speechtext:
With regard to a motion made by the hon.

Wheat Purchases
member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) for the production of certain information relating to the Canadian farm loan board, I am now tabling the answer to the question asked, but I should like to make a brief statement in regard to it.
On June 10 an order for return was tabled giving certain data in regard to applications received and loans granted by the British Columbia branch of the Canadian farm loan board, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for New Westminster. These data were given on a yearly basis, with a footnote stating that "the statistical records of the board are kept on a yearly basis." On June 11 the hon. member stated in the house that the answer to his question was an evasion of the question asked and requested me to bring the information down. At the time I promised to look into the matter and see whether the information was available on the basis asked for.
I have looked into the matter carefully and a statistical table has been prepared showing by months since January 1939 the number of applications for loans received, the number of loans granted, the amount of loans granted, and loan repayments, principal and interest. The original return was not an attempt to evade the question asked; it was merely an attempt to avoid what seemed to be unnecessary work on the part of the staff of the head office of the board, which has been depleted as a result of the war demands, and it was believed that any purpose which the hon. member might have had in mind would be served by the statistical information given. However, as the hon. member apparently regards it as fundamental to have the statistics on a monthly basis, they have been so compiled, and I am tabling herewith an amended return to the order that was tabled on June 10.

I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, which I would have asked him last week but for the fact that he was out of the city. It is based on an item appearing in the Winnipeg Tribune of June 23, as follows: Minister Says British Wheat Price Not Set Ottawa, June 23.-Trade Minister MacKinnon said Monday night no formal settlements have yet been made for British purchases of wheat in Canada.
This was the only comment he had to make on a Winnipeg report of an interview with
Professor J. Scott Watson, agricultural attache to the British embassy in Washington.
Professor Scott Watson said he understood British wheat purchases in Canada were being paid for by Canada out of the $1,000,000,000 gift to Britain fund.
To what period did the minister have reference, and did it include the three sales that he has announced in this house? I should like to know also whether the assumption made by Professor Scott Watson was correct.

maintopic: BRITISH PURCHASES IN CANADA-INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF PAYMENT
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: BRITISH PURCHASES IN CANADA-INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF PAYMENT
speechtext: This matter already has been the subject of answer by the minister, and if he wishes to reply now I think he would be in order in doing so.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: BRITISH PURCHASES IN CANADA-INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF PAYMENT
speechtext: I noticed the statement made in Washington, to which the hon. member refers. I had no notice of this question; otherwise I might have been able to give more detailed information. My statement to a representative of the Canadian Press was to the effect that according to my understanding, no formal settlement had been made by Britain for the wheat purchased last year from the Canadian wheat board. My understanding is that our sales to Britain are balanced to a certain extent by payments made, services given and goods shipped by the United Kingdom, but that no formal balancing of those accounts has been made as yet.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BRITISH PURCHASES IN CANADA-INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF PAYMENT
speechtext: That is only one part of it. What about the third question? Have our sales of wheat been paid for out of the billion dollar grant and will they be so paid for in the future? Surely the government has decided that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRITISH PURCHASES IN CANADA-INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say a word about that. Under the act providing for United Kingdom financing, the Dominion of Canada makes available to the United Kingdom a billion dollars for the purpose of purchasing munitions of war, foodstuffs and raw materials in Canada, and for defraying other expenses incurred in Canada by the United Kingdom. It is a little difficult to say whether any part of that billion dollars is applied to any particular commodity. The United Kingdom requires large sums in Canadian dollars for the purpose of purchasing goods in Canada, and they get those dollars in two ways. The first way is by the export of goods and the supplying of services and so on to Canada, which gives them several hundred million dollars. The second way is through the billion dollar gift. I have left out of account the $700,000,000 loan, but for the
Wheat Purchases

present fiscal period those are the two ways in which the United Kingdom obtain the dollars they require, and they use those dollars for the purchase of everything for which they require Canadian dollars, including wheat. But to say that any particular part of the billion dollars is allocated to the purchase of wheat is to say something which is impossible of demonstration. All the dollars which the United Kingdom must have for purchases in Canada are used for the purchase of goods, the obtaining of services, the construction of projects and remittances of one kind and another to Canada, and that total sum is made up in the two ways I have mentioned.

It goes on to give an excerpt from the speech I delivered the other evening, as follows:
Conscription was imposed on the people of Canada and particularly the province of Quebec m 1917, for no other reason than to win an election for a party which had lost the last vestige of the confidence of the people.

That extract from my remarks is followed by this statement:
So far is that statement from being true that it includes several misrepresentations. So far from conscription in 1917 being "imposed" on the people, a huge majority of the people did it themselves. And it was under a Union government in which the best of the Liberals of the day cooperated, except Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

subtopic: MR. MCDONALD, PONTIAC-REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN OTTAWA "JOURNAL" OF JUNE 29
speechtext: In connection with the passage of the Military Service Act during the session of 1917 I find the following to be the official record, which I should like to place upon Hansard in order to justify my statement and to prove that I am not guilty of falsifying the record. The bill was introduced by Sir Robert Borden and read the first time on June 11, 1917. It was read the second time in this house on July 6, 1917;. read a third time on July 24, 1917; passed by the senate on August 18, 1917, and received the royal assent on August 29, 1917. The Union government, to which this article refers, was sworn in on November 14, 1917; consequently it had absolutely nothing to do with the passing of the Military Service Act. I am entirely within my rights, I submit, in saying [DOT] that my reference to that matter was absolutely correct, and that I did not falsify the record.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, June 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. 80, to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Roy.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this debate has now lasted a considerable time. Much straw has been threshed out, and I trust I shall not impose on the house by speaking at too great length.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: No chaff?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I may not be a thresher, but if desirable I could speak at some length on that operation. I do feel, however, that it is my duty to make my position clear on this very important issue.
I am wholeheartedly in support of the bill now before the house and about, I trust, to receive its second reading. If I were not otherwise convinced, the events of the last fortnight would undoubtedly have convinced me that everything this country can do should be done *in prosecuting the war in every possible way. It is not a matter of courage on my part to take that attitude. I do think, however, that it required some courage on the

Mobilization Act-Mr. McLarty
part of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) to take the attitude he took in this house on Friday last.
I believe this measure is the natural and inevitable result of the plebiscite which was taken in April. Having thereby obtained the moral right to repeal section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act, I do not think we could do otherwise than take such legal right as lay within our power.
It has been suggested in various quarters that the vote was contingent on some precedent condition, that it might be conditioned on some modification of our monetary system, or upon the conscription of finance and industry. I prefer to believe that the question asked was fair and definite. It was made clear during the course of the plebiscite debate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made it amply clear, in his addresses on January 26 and February 25, and again in his radio addresses of April 7 and April 24, that the question meant exactly what it said, namely, that it was to give a moral right to take a course which at that time neither the government nor this house had the right to take.
My first reason for favouring the repeal of section 3 is that it constitutes a definite answer to and is the natural result of that plebiscite. That result is now well known. It might be well to put upon Hansard a few figures in connection with the vote taken on that occasion, a vote which by the way was the second largest ever taken in the history of Canada. The total vote was 4,638,847. The only other vote which was larger was that given in 1940, which surpassed this vote by approximately 43,000.
Rather than give the figures themselves I believe it might be more helpful if I gave the percentages by provinces and of the active service vote. The following figures refer to the "yes" vote:
Per cent
Prince Edward Island	 83-0
New Brunswick	 69-7
Nova Scotia	 78-5
Quebec	 27-5
Ontario	 83-8
Manitoba	 79'9
Saskatchewan	 71 -7
Alberta	 71-2
British Columbia	 80 T
Yukon territory	 73T
Yellowknife	 72-3
Canadian Service vote	 80-5
The total was an affirmative vote of 64-2 per cent.	[DOT]
There is one more reason why I approve definitely of the repeal of section 3. We have heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), from the various service ministers, from 
the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) of the work which Canada has been doing in connection with this war. Figures have been given to us which I believe indicate that this country is doing more per capita than any other of the united nations. But when we refer to the fact that we have expended $4,000,000,000, when we refer to the tremendous increase in the manufacture of aeroplanes, when we refer to the increase in our naval forces, when we refer to the production of all the mechanized units necessary for an army, the effect is lost in the opinion of the united nations because of the fact that section 3 still stands upon our statute book. The whole atmosphere is discoloured, the whole air is contaminated because that happens to be there. For that reason I believe it should be deleted, as is proposed in the bill now before this house.
There is another reason why I favour the deletion of this section. If we in Canada could elect where this war was to be fought we would have a tremendous advantage. But we cannot. Whether it will be fought in Alaska or in Newfoundland or in the British isles is not a matter for our decision; it is a matter for the decision of the enemy. Consequently I feel that we should be free to operate in every part of the world where operation seems to be necessary for the effective prosecution of the war. Suppose the congress of the United States had passed a measure in terms equivalent to section 3 of the act. All the splendid work they are doing in the production of the machines of war would be discounted. And would we not be critical? Would we not be suggesting that that was no effort on their part; that while the machines of war are necessary, while equipment for war is essential, these machines and equipment must necessarily be manned? If the congress of the United States passed such a measure as that what would be the reaction in this country?
I have already given the official returns, but may I suggest that there is perhaps an even stronger reason for adopting the measure we are now considering. It has been proved conclusively that the people of Canada are definitely in favour of the adoption of such a measure. That being so, and parliament being the servant of the people, can we do other than follow the verdict which has been given?
I remember being in Charlottetown about three years ago on the occasion of the celebration of the seventy-fifth anniversary of the Charlottetown convention of 1864. At that time I was impressed by the words on a

Mobilization Act-Mr. Rowe
bronze tablet, which words I imagine are familiar to most hon. members of this house. They were these:
Providence being their guide they builded better than they knew.
That was the foundation of our confederation. That was the union of the people of Canada. May I refer to my notes in order to state what I believe to be the significance of that union.
In our democratic system of government the evaluations include respect for special interests of groups and of minorities. This results in a balanced compromise which leads to the widest general agreement attainable. It was what John Stuart Mill called the greated good to the greatest number.
We are fighting for our existence-our very survival as a nation. What strategy of defence shall be adopted? The issue is whether the very conditions for the assertion of minority rights shall be lost or preserved. It is for the preservation of minority rights as essential constituents of our organization that we join issue with the enemy, and no group or individual has any social or political, to say nothing of constitutional, right to claim exemption from the duty inherently placed upon every citizen to give his all to preserve his own country's existence.
No minority, in any situation, in any place or at any time can claim the right to refuse to accept the legally ascertained judgment of the state as to the measures to be taken for its own salvation. It would be equivalent to a claim to a right to make that determination of strategy itself. Could any province claim to confine its own forces to its own boundaries? Or to Canada? And if not to Canada, what limitation can be placed on the decision constitutionally made? What is there in any conception of constitutionalism to give countenance to such a claim? Are we to stand on the shore till the enemy lands? Or meet him one mile, two miles, a thousand or two thousand miles, on land or sea? It is either that the strategy of preserving our state shall be confided absolutely to the majority, or that the minority shall have the right to pronounce upon all of us our own sentence of death.
My reference to the tablet in Charlottetown reminds me that perhaps we have been born in a somewhat unfortunate time. We have had to fight two wars, one to make the world safe for democracy and the other to preserve democracy in this world. But if we can pass on to our posterity the heritage which our forefathers have passed on to us, then I believe that in our day and generation we shall have done something of which we can long be proud.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up the time of this house at any great length.
I have listened with interest to the brief and somewhat emphatic but still uncertain utterances of the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty).
I agree with him to one extent, that there is not an hon. member within sound of my voice who has any doubt as to the issue that is at stake and who does not appreciate the seriousness of it during the recent weeks. When one realizes what has happened in Libya, when one remembers what happened in the mouth of the St. Lawrence river, when one realizes that the enemy has landed on the north American continent, when one realizes that only a few minutes ago we were told that the British forces had been driven back another sixty miles in Egypt, then he should have no doubt as to the seriousness of the situation and should pause and consider what is really happening.	_
Never has there been an issue so clear in the minds of the people, but never has there been an issue so confused in the halls of parliament. I doubt if at this late date in the debate I can do much in the way of clarification of it, but I assure you, sir, that I shall not add to the confusion already caused by the differences of opinion that exist in the minds of some sixty-seven supporters of the government who have spoken. I am glad to find myself in full accord and unison with the eleven speakers who have spoken on this debate from His Majesty's opposition. But as one listens to the speeches coming from the other side one cannot help but think that there are almost as many different policies in the government on this important issue as there were speakers. Together the government stand before the people, but divided they speak in parliament. We have heard a great deal about the importance of cabinet solidarity and unity in the government on important issues, but in the nineteen years in which it has been my privilege to attend this house, Mr. Speaker, I have not seen, and I doubt whether you have in the many years you have been in this house, such a muddled spectacle of disunity in the government party, the very party that has kept national unity on a political parade for the last twenty-five years.
I must not let this my first opportunity pass without complimenting and congratulating those in the government ranks who have submerged, as they believe, their political fortunes, or at least what are called their political interests, in order to respond to what they believed to be the challenge of duty at this time. I cannot help but refer to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), who made such a brilliant speech on Friday last, a man

Mobilization Act-Mr. Rowe
who has followed his party for so many years but who clearly and emphatically told this house and the country that in his mature judgment his party were not taking the stand on this issue which the people of the country believed they should.
Among the ministers we see disunity. But it is most fortunate indeed that we have the three ministers of defence standing four-square and independent of the attitude of the government, and I compliment them for their stand on this important issue. I admit that in normal times such a spectacle of disunity might call for further resignations from the government, but in time of war and grave crisis, when the enemy is hammering at both our doors, there is no one in this house who would suggest or even think of it at this time.
I believe in all sincerity that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), and the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) are struggling their very best at the present time to do a job, and I was further convinced of that when I heard them speak in this debate. I should like to compliment especially the Minister of National Defence for Air, the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). He was elected on far different slogans from those he proclaimed the other day, but with his eyes open to the effect his attitude might have on his political future he nevertheless chose to stand four-square behind our fighting men, including his own gallant son. His speech in this house last Thursday was a credit to his name, and I trust it will be an inspiration to his great old province of Quebec.
Despite the fact that the three ministers of defence have shown the way and taken their political lives in their hands, we find the remainder of the cabinet floundering and squirming, preferring to follow their leader's wait-and-see policy, refusing to look ahead. They prefer to blink at the war with one eye and wink at the ballot box with the other.
I hope they will look where they are going, instead of going where they are looking.
The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) claims that the emphasis on conscription has distorted our whole war effort, while the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) makes the brilliant suggestion that the merits of conscription are outweighed by its demerits. No one but himself knows what he means by that, but knowing his former opinion and remembering that he was one of the out-and-out isolationists, I have little confidence in his outlook on an all-out war effort.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has a heavy burden to carry. He perhaps does not know the past history of 
his party as well as some of those who are playing politics more viciously, and I therefore hesitate to mention him, especially when he is not in his seat. Quite innocently, I think, he said that the voluntary method was Canada's traditional method of raising men and the method best suited to the character of the people of this country. I do not agree with him. In the midst of his toil, and with that political innocence which he has so often demonstrated, he failed, I think, to realize the implications of his statement.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of course tells us that conscription for overseas may never be necessary. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) says that the present policy should be continued, and that conscription should not be brought into effect unless it was by a party that had no political past and no political future.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: He did not say that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Yes, he did, because I heard him. One need not be surprised at this amazing utterance by a responsible minister, because while the government has been following the middle-of-the-road policy, that was the policy the Minister of Agriculture advocated before the last election.
But it was the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) who made the most amazing statements on this issue. I realize that it was his first speech in this house; and I have a great respect for the hon. gentleman, who has built up for himself a very creditable record at the bar of his native province. But despite all the advantages with which he came here, no minister of justice in the nineteen years I have been in the house has ever left an important issue in more eloquent confusion than the present minister did when he concluded his speech on conscription. Indeed, had the debate concluded at that point, this indecisive government would have had to hold another plebiscite to ascertain whether we were to march forward as a British dominion or to halt as a French colony. I listened to the minister's statement that-
-our loyalty cannot be expected to be one of traditional affection and sentiment, but it is one based almost solely on a utilitarian viewpoint.
He was repeating a statement he had made in 1939 and he quoted it in this debate at page 3391 of Hansard. What a utilitarian viewpoint may mean to a lawyer I do not know.
I am a farmer. It might mean cost plus ten per cent, or it might mean freedom and privileges paid for by somebody else. That might not be the meaning given to it in a court of law, but it is the meaning given to it by the

Mobilization Act-Mr. Rowe
farmers of my constituency. The minister went on to say:
It may be great and glorious to fight and die for the world's salvation, for the salvation of the united nations-
What are we, Mr. Speaker, but one of the united nations? Does he wish us to cease to be a member of the united nations? He went on:
-but that is a privilege of each man, a privilege he has the right to choose for himself-
That is a privilege-for the boys to fly with their loads of bombs over Libya and over Egypt, or to stand and fight with their backs to the wall at Singapore and Hong Kong- that is a pleasant privilege!
-a privilege he has the right to choose for himself; it is not a duty which citizenship imposes as an obligation correlative to the rights which citizenship guarantees as a privilege.
I have always felt that I was a Canadian citizen and also a British subject, and that as a British subject I had some duty to my king and my empire, to the British commonwealth of nations, and, to-day, to the united nations to which the minister referred, which are engaged in a fight to the death against the most terrible enemy that civilization has ever faced. How, then, can we adopt the position taken by the minister?
The Globe and Mail, whose accuracy I have no reason to doubt, though at times they have not agreed with me, also report on the same day the Minister of Justice as having said this, speaking in the house:
French-speaking Canadians have no sentimental attachment for the government of the British isles.
I do not know whether the fact that that passage does not appear in Hansard indicates that the minister does not feel that way about it. But it has been my privilege during my experience in public life to have known some of the finest French Canadians in this country, both in Ontario and in Quebec: I have talked in Montreal and Quebec to leading French Canadians, and I doubt very much the correctness of the minister's statement, despite his long residence in Quebec, that French Canadians have no sentimental attachment to the government of the British isles, or even to British imperialism, in view of the privileges which they have enjoyed and which were conferred upon them under the British flag. Thousands of French Canadians died in the last great war. Many are fighting and dying valiantly in the present war along with their Anglo-Saxon fellow-citizens. I talked not long ago in Montreal to a French Canadian who was appalled at the representation which 44561-237
his province had received on the floor of this house. He said, "I fought throughout the last war, and my three brothers are fighting in this war; one failed to return from Dunkirk, and another was unable to get away from Greece. I feel," he said, "that if we do not stand together now, we shall fall apart." I realize, as one of the majority race in this country, the necessity of having tolerance at all times towards one another. But I say to my fellow-Canadians from Quebec: You have gone a long way in your efforts to dictate the policy of this dominion. We have every desire to recognize your rights, specifically with regard to your religion and your schools, guaranteed under the British North America Act; but there is nothing in that act or in *the constitution of Canada since confederation which gives any minority the right to dictate the policy of the majority of the people of this dominion. I say that in all kindness, because I do not propose to say anything here or anywhere else in Canada that will hurt the feelings of that other great race of people in this dominion, the French Canadian. But I do say that it is unfair to the great French-Canadian race to have them represented as having no interest in the world conflict outside the shores of Canada, when we know, and they know, that on the result of it depends the liberty of their religion-which is no dearer to them than my religion is to me- the right of free worship, the right of free assembly. We shall not continue to enjoy these rights until we meet the realities which press so urgently for attention. But here we flounder along, trying to find a solution of a matter which the people in the country have already decided for us. It is unfortunate that, evidently for political reasons, one province should be misled and placed in an unfavourable light by those who represent her here. French-speaking Canadians have, I believe, a sentiment of sympathy with the British empire. These ministers, Mr. Speaker, fail to realize, in their pursuit of a policy which puts one province in opposition to the wishes of the rest, that minority rights are secure only so long as the minority enjoys the tolerant good will of the majority. That is a long-existent rule in this country; indeed it is a rule in any country. The majority of the people of Canada expressed themselves in favour of an all-out war effort, and the majority expect an all-out war effort. Because two-thirds of the voters in one province oppose that policy, is their will to prevail against the expressed wishes of an affirmative majority, no less emphatic, in the eight other provinces?
I have been a member of this house for some years. I believe my record shows that

Mobilization Act-Mr. Rowe

I have been motivated by no feelings of intolerance, and that I have endeavoured to show good will to my friends in Quebec of another race. But I realize what we have gone through and what lies ahead of us, and I believe that we shall not meet the future successfully unless all of us stand together in the present crisis. What is the use of blowing trumpets and talking about national unity on election campaign platforms? "National unity" has been paraded up and down this country; it is the most hackneyed political phrase I know of; it has been the stock-in-trade of the Liberal party in this dominion for a quarter of a century. What is unity? What is its worth if we cannot stand together now, when almost the whole world is against us? We had better know now whether we are to be divided or not. In times of peace, when everything is going well, unity is easy. Now is the time when national unity means something more than filling ballot boxes. Now is the time when we must decide whether we shall have in future decisions by ballots or decisions by bullets. Now is the time to capitalize and utilize the "national unity" which we have been parading for the past twenty-five years, and to see whether it is to be expressed in action by every man who loves the freedom of his own faith- that freedom which my friends of Quebec have so long enjoyed-and the privileges enjoyed by his race, given to that race, after the conquest of years gone by, by the most tolerant power in the world-the British empire-and enjoyed under that flag; for under no other could they have been enjoyed so long and so securely.
Now that we are facing this crisis, I want to ask whether we are to work our own defeat by following policies of disunity. President Lincoln said during the civil war in the United States that a nation divided against itself cannot stand. Those words should echo and reecho in this building and throughout this country at the present time. As Canadians we must face the realities of war, and in such an attitude there is no place for disunity. It must be recognized that the present condition is far removed from that all-out war effort which is needed.
The only hope I can see is that those who prefer to blink at the war with one eye and wink at the ballot box with the other may eventually look where they are going rather than go where they are looking. At any rate I know that no less responsible men than the Prime Minister and his cabinet are worried about what is happening in other countries. I realize that an emissary of the government has been sent to the United States in order to
EMr. Rowe.]
improve the reports that are given out about the Canadian war effort. I know from visiting the United States occasionally that there is reason to be alarmed at the present state of Canada's one-time prestige in the great republic to the south. No doubt the Prime Minister has been concerned, as he has mentioned at different times in this house. One has only to read an editorial such as that reprinted the other day in the Toronto Globe and. Mail from a United States paper, which stated:
If the Canadian government expects to enjoy the respect of the American people it will have to impose conscription on a par with America. The Canadian government has a record of so scrupulously respecting minority rights, of coddling a pampered child so long, that failure to impose equal conscription will appear more and more as an effort on its part to place its own personal political welfare ahead of that of victory and have American people assume burdens which it should assume without further fear.
That, Mr. Speaker, is why the American people are concerned; that is why the British people are concerned-not because of the attitude of a province of this dominion, not because of the attitude of a gallant race in this dominion-I hope my friends in the province of Quebec, including the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), do not misunderstand me. The reason is that we have this everlasting search for political expediency, even in a time of crisis, which destroyed our plans for an air training scheme in 1938, which has already cost the lives of thousands of boys overseas, which has left us so that the empire does not know where we are going and the United States do not know whence we are coming. I urge that we should stop, look and listen, and awaken to the parade before the world marches by. I have heard no less a man that the late minister of justice, an honoured representative of the province of Quebec-who was, I am proud to say, a very close friend of mine for many years; I always felt at home in his office or wherever I met him-I have heard him speak in days past, and while I never heard him go quite so far as some speakers have in this debate, I recall that on one occasion he went so far as to say that this country had won a new status through a visit of the Prime Minister of Canada and himself overseas. He said: "We have all the status and sovereign right of a state in the British empire." He said: "I see in the distance only a fine silken thread binding us to the empire." He added that the silken thread was still strong, and he was reminded of how that status was secured. It was not secured by the present Prime Minister in those days when he was fol-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Rowe
lowing his economic appeasement policies throughout the world. It was not achieved by that right hon. gentleman, the great compromiser and reconciler, whether in his own party or in international affairs. It was achieved by the blood of the boys who fought in the last war. As the late Sir Robert Borden said in 1918, "When I signed that treaty I felt the tears roll down my cheeks because I knew that I was writing the new status of Canada with the blood of the boys who sleep in Flanders' fields." "Lest we forget". How will the future prestige of this empire and the future security of this dominion be written? Will it be by the men of my riding who work behind the plough, sixteen hours a day for the fixed prices that the government has imposed on them? Will it be by the man who works in a war industry, or by the army of men carrying on a bureaucratic administration?-necessarily, I admit, in some measure. No; it will be written with the blood of the men behind the guns, and the sooner we realize that the better.
When we roll off the lines thousands and thousands of tanks and aeroplanes and turn out great numbers of machine guns and trench mortars, let us not forget that we shall need that many more men to use them if we are going to win this war. We shall probably meet with certain reverses. We shall probably have to endure some shelling of Halifax, or bombing of Vancouver island, or sinkings in the gulf of St. Lawrence, or other sporadic attacks by the enemy, but to win the war we shall have to start an offensive over where my hon. friend would not admit was any part of our defence, namely, on the western front. That is why there are more-my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) might think I was going to say something I should not; but I will say this, that the American people realize to-day that if we are going to win this war it must be won overseas in Europe, and that is why they are conscripting their men to put them in the British Isles. Is it to watch their isles in the Pacific that have been taken one by one, to watch the Aleutian islands or the Oregon coast, which was fired on the other day? No; because they realize that, as in any other fight, if we are to win we must meet the enemy oi. common ground.

Do the other ministers not agree with the three ministers of national defence, each of whom says the same thing-that Canada's defence is overseas? We are standing at the crossroads of our fate. We must realize that the enemy is ready to strike us if our boys over there let them pass. Those boys stand and say, "They shall not pass", but if they did pass I would like to see what sized army would stop them on the banks of the St. Lawrence. I do not think my hon. friend would prefer to fight them in Saskatchewan rather than overseas. The hour has struck; the time is long past when we should fool away the time of this house as has been done. And it is not the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) or other groups on this side that have held up this debate. We have had sixty-seven speeches from the other side of the house, and the more they talk the less one understands where the government is going. The more speeches they make the more pages they add to another chapter of the story of confusion at which Canada is becoming more and more amazed.

speechtext:
I should not be surprised if it were better than most, but it would be even less confusing if the hon. member would come and sit over here where he should sit, with the ideas he has on this war issue.
I say in all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, that we have reached a critical point in the history of this country. I warn the government that there is a difference between rigid control of those who hinder the war effort and the persecution by a gestapo of those who criticize the government for its lack of war effort. I
Mobilization Act-Mr. Rowe

am not mentioning any names, but when I see my deskmate hit over the head and knocked down, and another hon. member liable to the same treatment if he is not careful, I wonder how long this situation is going to continue. I do not know as much about law as the Minister of Justice knows, but I wonder how much I could say before he would intern me. I suggest that there is a tendency in this country that might well be feared by more than the individual, because history has told us, in shocking stories of the past, that when the rights of the individual have been "ges-tapoed" the freedom of the press is restricted very shortly thereafter. I warn my friends of the press gallery to watch their fast pens these days, because several newspapers are vigorously condemning the government because of its war effort, or lack of it; they are wondering why the government is floundering in this way, what it is waiting for, and so on. They wonder why some of the cabinet say the enemy is overseas and our only defence is over there, while others say we must stay here and fight, while still others say they are not sure we should be in the war at all.
Is it any wonder that the people are rapidly losing confidence in our government? They are losing confidence because they expect courageous leadership in time of crisis. They are losing confidence because they expect determined action against a vicious enemy. They are losing confidence because they expect definite, clear and united purpose in a responsible government. They are losing confidence because the government required a plebiscite to tell them what to do, and more confidence because the government will not do it after being told to do it. We have never seen such a spectacle of uncertainty, confusion, distress, disunity and turmoil in a government; and this government has more members behind it than any other government since confederation. We were twitted when we asked for a national government, no doubt because the administration figured they had behind them people of every stripe of politics, as a result of the disunity which they have brought about, and which they probably felt constituted the only form of national government they could have.
In conclusion I want to say only that we are going to win this w-ar in spite of the government. The prestige of this dominion will be upheld by our boys who have enlisted in the armed forces, God bless them; and the future status of this country will be determined by those boys, not by some glib lawyers who will tell us about it in the years to come. It will not be determined by a floundering,

fearful sort of attitude, such as the government has adopted. It will not be determined by an attitude such as that of the Minister of National War Services, or that of the Minister of Agriculture. It will be determined by attitudes such as those of the hon. member for Ontario, the Minister of National Defence for Air, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services and the Minister of National Defence. This war will not be won by any single political party.

God save our king and heaven bless The maple leaf forever.
My hon. friend laughs. This war will be won by those who appreciate and understand that the privileges and rights they have enjoyed in the past have been given them by that veiy power, now threatened, the British commonwealth of nations, which forms part of the united nations, standing with that half of our civilization that believes in defending freedom instead of surrendering it as other countries did who thought it was not their duty to go beyond their shores until the enemy invaded them.

Mobilization Act-Mr. McKinnon
