speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard many excellent speeches during this debate, covering practically all the important points, and with few exceptions those who have spoken have been very considerate and tolerant of the viewpoints of others. We often look back and think how outstanding were the fathers of confederation, how tolerant and understanding they were, with vision that has brought Canada to the position she occupies to-day. But when, everything is considered I believe the speech of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) last Friday shows that we still have giants among us, and the future of Canada is well assured as long as we have men of that calibre in the public life of this country.
As I see it, this bill is simply the legal completion of the recent plebiscite. Ordinarily it would be more or less a routine matter, but in view of certain developments it has been given a position of importance that few of us could have imagined a short time ago. The bill has been thoroughly discussed; all points in connection with it have been well brought out, and I see no reason to discuss it further. There are a few remarks I should like to make, however, which might be of material benefit to the welfare of the country and to the war effort as a whole.
Between Fort William and Winnipeg there is a territory covering some 430 miles in which as yet this government has not seen fit to establish any war industries. The government would be well advised to take a leaf out of the book of Russia and establish industries in that territory, which is practically the geographical centre of Canada, because they would be as far away from any possible military action as they could be placed in Canada.
I should like to commend the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) upon his approval of employer-employee council. That is an excellent idea, and it was only recently that Mr. E. M. Little strongly endorsed the minister's stand. Mr. Little on that occasion said he did not believe all the brains of the country were in the front office. With that I thoroughly agree. Not only should we make use of all the physical abilities of our citizens, but we should use their mental abilities also. With the establishment of these councils we will go a long way toward assisting to put our war effort on an all-out basis. The government should go further and insist that the councils be established in at least the war industries of the country.
There are many matters affecting my constituency I should like to discuss, but I do not believe such discussion would be proper
in this debate. There will be other appropriate occasions on which matters of vital importance to my constituency may be brought up. I would point out, however, that the people of Kenora-Rainy River voted thirteen to one in favour of the plebiscite. There never was any question in my mind as to what they would do, if given an opportunity. They have given every possible assistance in the war effort.
Voluntary enlistments from my constituency in this war, as in the last one, are exceptionally high and compare favourably with those of any other part of Canada. The people of Kenora-Rainy River have subscribed heavily to recent loans. When they voted thirteen to one in the affirmative there could be no doubt in my mind as to the meaning they meant to convey. I am definitely in favour of national selective service, and I propose to vote in support of the bill. I should prefer to vote on the details in connection with conscription, but I well realize it may be impossible to give the house an opportunity to do so. Therefore I concede that the government should have the right by order in council to bring in conscription at such time as they deem it necessary. No man, no body of men, no newspaper, in my opinion has the necessary information upon which to base an opinion as to when the conscription of man-power should take place. That would be a duty for the government to perform.
As has been pointed out by various ministers, there are many activities, including agricultural development and the production of munitions, which go to make up our total contribution to the war effort. Only the government know the extent of what has been done, and because of that they are the only body in a position to know when a policy of conscription should be made effective.
Speaking a few days ago, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) pointed out that a shortage of man-power was definitely possible. In that he is no doubt correct. I believe, however, that there is plenty of man-power employed in non-essential work which could and should be used in our war effort. Let none of us have any illusions about what we are up against. As I see it, this is a war of extermination. Either we win or we go down where there will be no future for the people of this country. It takes very little thought on my part to decide the proper course, because we have no choice. The issue is as clear as it can be. We either go all-out in fighting our enemies wherever they may be found, or we wait until it is too late.
My family have not waited. All who could go have gone, and I am like-minded. The

Mobilization Act

Mr. Edwards
people generally in the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River feel that no price is too great to pay for what has to be done.
May I make one suggestion? If and when the government decides that conscription is necessary, I suggest it should set a date, by proclamation or otherwise after which no more volunteers will be accepted. All enlistments from then on should be on a selective service basis. In my opinion that would be fair both to the individual and to the country generally.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Let me say at the outset that I am wholeheartedly in favour of the bill, and will vote for it. My interest in the subject matter of the bill goes back to the evening of September 3, 1939, when I, in common with my fellow Canadians, heard the fateful news over the radio at four o'clock in the morning, mountain time, that Germany had invaded Poland.
How well do I remember the emotions I experienced, which completely changed my thinking processes! For be it known that at that hour on that morni' g I was laboriously preparing a speech I had expected to deliver in a by-election to be held in September in the constituency of Calgary West. My reaction to the news was such that every partisan or political thought I had entertained was completely obliterated. Matters which seemed of paramount consideration in connection with the winning of the by-election paled into insignificance before the awful thought that our empire was at war. I for one never doubted that my country, my Canada, would take up the sword in defence of liberty and freedom, and against dictatorship and oppression.
A by-election was held in September and I felt so keenly about what had taken place that on the morning of September 3 I wired the government and gave it as my considered opinion that I should withdraw from the byelection to make way for the Conservative candidate in a seat which with one exception had been Conservative from its inception. This was the seat of none other than the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. It was somewhat of a disappointment, a blow to personal aspirations, but I felt that under the existing circumstances it was the right thing to do, despite the fact that my supporters might misunderstand and my political enemies misconstrue the reasoning behind my decision. A Conservative was returned again from Calgary West. But I was justified in the sacrifice, if you will, which I made at that time, by subsequently being honoured by the same people in the spring of 1940 with their endorsation and elec-

tion to this house. One of the things uppermost in my mind at that time was the realization that the people of Canada, and particularly the political leaders of Canada, would not wish to be confronted, when they were making up their minds as to what stand they should take in this world conflict, by the lesser consideration as to whether or not there should be the conscription of man-power for overseas service.
I could not help but recall the feelings by which I was actuated when at the time of the last war I did eveiything I could to gain admission to the fighting services. For the life of me I cannot understand any red-blooded Canadian of military age not having the promptings which I experienced at that time and the desire to go out and fight for his king and country. I have little sympathy with the individual who justifies his refusal to serve as is commonly done these days, on the ground that some other fellow will get his job, that some other young man has not done his part or has not offered to do his part, or that some other section or class, or creed if you will, is not doing its fair share. This is the greatest crisis that has ever confronted mankind, and there can be no such thing as equality of service or sacrifice. Nothing that I can do or give can weigh against the sacrifice of that friend of mine and yours who lays down his life for Canada and the cause for which we fight? There has been a lot of false reasoning and false logic spread abroad in our land to the effect that this is a war for the defence of Canada or the defence of the British empire. I do not believe that the gallant lads whom I knew and whom I taught at school, the men with whom I grew up and have been associated in later years, are in this fight solely for the defence of any particular part of the terrestrial globe, let alone any of that part of the globe which is generally shown in pink and labelled in black letters "Canada."
Surely there is something finer and grander than the defence of a piece of ground. I believe the Canadian people, and certainly the brave lads who wear uniforms, whether they are serving in the air, on land or on the sea, feel that there is something greater at stake. What is it? The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated what I trust we all believe to be true-that the real issue in this struggle is our way of life and living; it is democracy versus dictatorship; it is freedom and liberty versus slavery. To put this struggle on any other plane is to belittle the objectives and the issues for which we are fighting. Surely we are not in this war merely to defend Canada. Surely the members of this house and the people of Canada realize that if you

Mobilization Act-Mr. Edwards
took all the man-power and all the production of which this country is capable in the way of munitions, food and everything else, there would not be sufficient to defend Canada successfully against the aggressor nations, any more than it would be possible for one prairie farmer to protect his farm against the onslaught of a prairie fire. This is a world on fire, and we are committed to something greater, to something finer, and I trust to something grander, than merely the defence of our own country.
People fight against things. We are fighting against dictatorship, world domination and slavery. We are not fighting for any thing, place or possession; we work for a better world; we fight against that which would destroy it. Men and women the world over will put forth their best efforts when it is realized that they are fighting against something, not fighting for something.
I should say at the outset that as a theory and as a principle of war policy, I have favoured compulsory selective service not only with respect to man-power but with respect to every resource this country possesses. I realize, however, that not until the national resources mobilization bill was introduced was there a decided opposition to that principle in certain sections of the country. Theoretically I do not see how a democracy can wage total war without recourse to that principle, but in practice I recognize the difficulties of applying it in Canada, by reason of views and opinions held with regard to it by many others.
Be it said that conscription- was not an election issue in 1940 in my constituency. There was, however, later, a group in Calgary, to which the Prime Minister has adverted on other occasions in favour of compulsory military service, and it was in that city that he first encountered an organized demand for conscription for overseas service. At that time I felt, and I believe the people of Calgary still feel, that the meetings which were then organized were largely called together by a political pressure group which was endeavouring at that time to sow political discord and disharmony and bring the government of the day into disrepute. There were others, however, and of this I am certain, who were greatly concerned and agitated lest their loved ones overseas should be unsupported.
I for one welcomed the introduction of the .plebiscite. I worked during that campaign and was not a little pleased that my constituency, despite handicaps imposed by war restrictions with respect to transportation facilities, and the fact that nobody's political "hide" was at stake, turned out and voted to the number of 19,715 persons as compared
with 19,798 persons at the general election. In other words the number of voters was only eighty-three short of the number of voters there had been at the general election in the spring of 1940. Of those who voted, 17,612 voted affirmative, 1,976 negative, and there were 127 spoiled ballots. During that campaign I stated what I then and theretofore believed and still believe to be the democratic, the fair, the just, the ideal and perfect way of mobilizing our resources, including our manpower, namely, by compulsory selective service. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read a few paragraphs from the statement I gave to the press just before the plebiscite was taken:
As a government policy, I believe in compulsory selective service or conscription. As an individual citizen neither you nor I are called upon by this plebiscite to declare whether or not we believe in conscription for overseas service NOW. The best opinion, that is the opinion of those who are charged with the responsibility of conducting this phase of our war effort, say that conscription is not necessary AT THIS TIME but that emergencies may arise at any time when it may be necessary to resort to compulsion,' and it is in anticipation of such an emergency that parliament, and by that I mean the representatives of every political party, is asking that it be released from this promise.
And I gave three reasons why they should vote:
1.	You are not called on by this plebiscite to declare whether or not you believe in conscription for overseas service.
2.	You are not called on to vote for or against the government.
3.	You are not called on to decide any question other than whether the government should be free to adopt any policy that may become necessary to ensure victory.
Then I concluded my statement with these two paragraphs:
To refuse to vote or to vote "no" is to declare in effect that no matter what emergency may face the country no one should be compelled under any circumstances to defend Canada in any field of action beyond the limits of this dominion, that no one should be called on to strike a blow for his country until the enemy has landed or is about to land on its shores.
I urge all thoughtful Canadians that they should by an overwhelming affirmative vote put their representatives in a position to be free to act and urge the adoption of whatever methods or measures may be required to attain victory in the uncertain and perilous days which lie ahead.
I am grateful and pleased that my electors, my friends, the people of Calgary West, have released me from any pledge, though indeed I needed no release from any pledge except that which was impliedly given by me as a supporter of this government in regard to that one phase of Canada's war effort.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Edwards
The plebiscite having passed, may I say that there will be nothing but resentment, if this government gives my constituents cause for believing that it entertains any idea of retreating from the position which it took at the outset, that this war is more than a war for the defence of Canada, that it is in very truth a war for an ideal, a war for the defence of democracy and freedom, a war for our way of life and of living. I was proud as a Canadian to learn that not only the people of my constituency but the people of Canada generally voted overwhelmingly to release the government from its commitment as embodied in clause 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act, to delete which the present bill has been introduced. This bill will, as I believe the people of Canada wish it to do, remove the last and only legislative restriction upon our all-out war effort.
I for one cherish the thought and the hope that never again in the political history of this fair dominion will any statesman feel called upon or obliged to make a promise such as, unquestionably, the leaders of the three major political parties made at the outset of this war. From now on the government has a clear mandate to take any and every action which in its considered opinion is calculated to increase in strength and effectiveness the power of this nation, working in the closest cooperation possible with every other nation having the same objectives.
To my hon. friends from Quebec may I say that the people of western Canada, at least in that part of it in which I have lived for the last thirty years, and especially the men of my age and generation find it extremely difficult to appreciate or understand, or even to view with tolerance, the attitude and ideas to which we have listened in this house. I have been much agitated and, indeed, nonplussed for months to try to discover the causes which lie behind the feeling and views to which we have listened during the last month or six weeks in the debate on this bill. Surely, my French-Canadian friends, you do not appreciate or understand the significance of what is going on in the world about you. Why should you be so alert and so anxious to defend our own country when perforce, by modern means of transportation, London and Liverpool, France and even Germany are closer to you than British Columbia or even parts of my province? And it is there the enemy should and, please God, will be destroyed.
I want to pay tribute to one man in this house from Quebec who, to my way of thinking, has given us an outstanding example of *<Mr, Edwards.]
singleness of purpose and devotion to the call of conscience and duty in the speech which he delivered here on Friday last. I refer to the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr, Power). I am sure that the people throughout the length and breadth of Canada will applaud his actions and his words, which can be likened only to those of another great leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who came from his province and wrho was willing, at a time of national peril, to take his political future in his hands, vote according to the dictates of his conscience, and govern his actions accordingly.
By any standard, whether of men, money or munitions, Canada's war effort has been adjudged good. The sole question which should concern this house and the Canadian people is, can it be made better, more efficiently effective? Mere size, bulk or numbers, whether of persons, munitions, money or other things, means little in this day and generation when pitted against skill, science and knowledge.
The government has asked to be relieved of its promise. The people of Canada have answered most emphatically that it should be so relieved. I believe that the future conduct of this war can safely be entrusted to the members of the cabinet, headed by our worthy Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). We have, and I believe the world has, confidence in the Prime Minister; confidence, not only in his judgment, but in his singleness of purpose and his anxious desire that this country shall take its proper place among the nations of the world and do its utmost in the struggle. We have confidence in our Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley); in our Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe); in our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner); and in our three national defence ministers. Is there any doubt or misgiving, on the part of anyone who has followed the careers of these hon. gentlemen in the house and before the public, as to their determination that this nation shall put forth the maximum of which it is capable? Theirs will be the decision. They have asked to be empowered; and I for one, not only reflecting the views of my constituents but giving expression to my personal convictions, am satisfied that they will never shrink from their clear duty, nor pause in their efforts until this country is making its maximum war effort.
As a school boy I learned this verse which has stuck with me throughout the years. I* believe they are the words of a great Nova Scotian statesman and patriot, and I commend them to the consideration of this house as an ideal which should animate and inspire every loyal Canadian. I think it goes like this:

Mobilization Act-Mr. d'Anjou
Inheritors of glory! 0 countrymen we swear To guard the flag that o'er thee Shall onward Victory bear.
Where e'er through earth's far regions Its triple crosses fly,
For God, for home, our kinsmen Shall win, or fighting die.
With that as our objective, with that as our motto, this country cannot fail.
Mr. J. E. S. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I opposed the plebiscite bill because I believed that such a measure would lead to conscription for overseas service, as later events have borne out. During a memorable meeting held in my constituency on April 16 last, I declared that perhaps within two weeks of the plebiscite vote, provided it were affirmative, a measure would be introduced in the House of Commons calling for conscription for overseas service. And I was right. As a matter of fact on May 10, Bill No. SO appeared on the order paper and the house was thereby requested to strike out section 3 of the 1940 mobilization act, thus extending compulsory service to overseas. That is the measure we are now discussing, Mr. Speaker.
When I had the honour of being elected as member for Rimouski in 1917, I gave the undertaking that I would oppose any conscription measure submitted to parliament, whatever government were in power. In 1940, the voters of Rimouski again did me the honour of choosing me as their representative. I gave them my solemn pledge that I would even break with my party if that party undertook to enforce conscription for overseas service. Indeed, and I wish to repeat this, I vigorously opposed the plebiscite bill when it was introduced in the house. I voted against it because I believed that it merely served to mask the evil face of conscription. As I have said, events bore me out.
Mr. Speaker, I must adhere to the stand I had previously taken and declare from the very outset that I shall vote against Bill No. 80 because this measure is synonymous with conscription for overseas service. In my humble opinion, the present government is acting even more dangerously than that of 1917 because it desires to introduce conscription not only with the concurrence of the people's representatives but at its own discretion by order in council. In 1917, the union government introduced a conscription bill for overseas service and the measure was discussed for three weeks. Well do I recall the titanic struggle then waged by two regretted leaders of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Ernest 44o61-238
Lapointe. We sat night and day to try to prevent the passing of that bill. That is why I wonder at the moment why the Liberal party which has endeavoured for the last twenty-five years, particularly in my province, to show that it was irrevocably opposed to conscription, now wishes to introduce a conscription measure, and1 that by order in council. As I stated a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, I opposed conscription in 1917 and I do so again to-day. I deeply regret that it should be the Liberal party that wishes to saddle us with this coercive legislation in 1942. You may be sure that the people of my province, the people of Quebec, are surprised, to say the least, at the Liberal government's present stand.
I followed attentively the speeches delivered by hon. members who spoke before me this afternoon. They seemed mainly to assail the attitude of the province of Quebec. Even if Quebec did cast a negative vote on the plebiscite, a close study of the figures for the other provinces shows that some six to seven hundred thousand negative votes were cast. The province of Quebec seems to be the bugbear of certain hon. members of this house. Yet I think that since the outbreak of the war, Quebec has contributed her full share and continues to do so. During the last war two Victoria Crosses were awarded to soldiers from my constituency. Which goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that the constituency of Rimouski is not peopled by cowards and poltroons. Jean Brillant and Joseph Keable were volunteers who fought overseas. They must have proved outstandingly brave since the Victoria Cross is the highest decoration awarded by His Majesty the King. At the present time, Rimouski has a training camp where even farmers' sons report for military service and also an air force training centre at Mont Joli. I therefore feel our citizens are doing their duty and that the criticisms levelled at the province of Quebec are no more warranted in the case of Rimouski than in the case of other constituencies.
Mr. Speaker, a great deal has been said about national unity. It seems that Quebec is always expected to sacrifice everything for the sake of national unity. In our Canadian confederation Quebec secured some rights which she intends to uphold. We insist that they be recognized. We are being asked continuously to ensure national unity and to that end it is we who must always yield, who must forego the rights guaranteed us by confederation. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, my province has done her full share in the Canadian confederacy and we of Quebec

Mobilization Act-Mr. d'Anjou

should not be alone in forsaking our privileges. We must all do our part if we wish to remain united.
In the interest of Canada's defence, I would agree to every sacrifice. We are told that this country will be better defended overseas. The assertion has never been proved. Our country is open to attacks by Germany or Japan on both our coasts and I fear that the government has not devoted sufficient time to the organization of our defences. Yet we have before us Australia's sad experience. Her shock troops fought in Greece and elsewhere and when Australia was attacked, she had to beg for help from the United States. I consider that Canada's war effort has been adequate so far and, as I was saying, I have always opposed coercive methods of dispatching troops overseas. My electors have given me a mandate which I will fulfil by voting against Bill No. 80.
In my opinion, the government has introduced this bill as a sop to the extremist faction in this country. Speeches are delivered in this house by members who will never have to go to war, who have no children, and who, like certain Toronto people, only see in conscription an avenue leading to larger profits. The province of Quebec will be the most affected by conscription for overseas service, because of her larger families. I myself come from a family of fifteen children, which included twelve sons. Families of eight, nine or ten sons are by no means scarce in my constituency. If this conscription bill passes, it will affect us more than the rest of Canada. Moreover, Canada has a population of only 11,000,000. Has not Canada's war effort been adequate so far as compared with that of more populous countries?
This bill is not justified and the government has not, to my mind, been released from its commitments or pledges of 1940. The late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe declared in this house: "Never will the province of Quebec submit to conscription". That was the agreement entered into at the time of the declaration of war. With Mr. Lapointe, the ministers who represented the province of Quebec stated: "We will participate in the war on condition that conscription for overseas service is never enforced". The province of Quebec voted for the upholding of the pledges given, and moreover a large number of people in other sections did the same, as I said a moment ago. For twenty-five years, the Liberal party has conducted all its election campaigns, not only in the dominion but in the provincial field, on a 
"no conscription" platform. As I have said, it sought to give, especially to the province of Quebec, the impression that the Liberal party was the only one opposed to conscription. After placing our confidence in the present Prime Minister who, with the help of Mr. Lapointe and all the members from Quebec, was chosen in 1919 to succeed Sir Wilfrid Laurier, I wonder whether it cannot be considered a betrayal of our province to seek to introduce a measure involving conscription for overseas service, in spite of the verdict given on April 27 last.
In politics as in anything else, Mr. Speaker, one must abide by one's pledges. In 1940, every political party was against conscription. The people returned this government with the largest majority ever obtained in our history. It is not enough to claim that conditions have changed. Conditions may have changed but the pledges remain. I for one cannot see any reason for supporting the bill now before the house. It is all well and good for certain hon. members of this house, as I said before, to urge conscription when they will not themselves take part in the war and when they have no sons of military age. As regards our war effort, the province of Quebec has answered the call voluntarily and perhaps much better than certain other provinces of the dominion, and I cannot understand why some hon. members of this house find it impossible to speak without criticizing the province of Quebec.
There is no cause to defend the province of Quebec. She is doing her duty just as she has done in the past. She acquitted herself well in 1917. She has discharged her obligations from 1939 to this date, and this incessant carping on her war effort should cease. I for one criticize no other province. However, as a citizen of Quebec, I have a perfect right to protest strongly against the insinuations of cowardice and ill-will directed against my province by some hon. members.
The province of Quebec is as loyal to her king as she is to the country and I claim for my part that my fellow citizens' first loyalty is to Canada. My motto is that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier: "Canada first, Canada always and Canada only." It sounds fine to say that we should meet the enemy wherever he may be. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, in a struggle such as this, where millions of men are locked in battle, where mechanized forces, tanks and planes are of supreme importance, why run the risk of disturbing the peace of this country by sacrificing through a conscription measure for overseas service between two and three hundred thousand men to the enemy's land and aerial onslaught. Infantry

Mobilization Act-Mr. d'Anjou
will not be the deciding factor in this war. It has been shown to date that victory will be won through tanks and aeroplanes. I therefore repeat that it would be a national crime to enact this law of conscription at the risk of destroying national unity, in order to raise perhaps two or three thousand men to be sent overseas as cannon fodder. This war will not be won by masses of men. While millions and millions of men are now taking part in the conflict, the present war is chiefly a mechanized one where tanks and aeroplanes will finally decide the issue.
I believe that the government has been ill-advised. Moreover it has no mandate to impose conscription for overseas service. It has not been released from its commitments. Not only did the province of Quebec refuse to release the government from its pledges against conscription, but there were at least six or seven hundred thousand Canadian citizens in other provinces who voted likewise. When speaking on the plebiscite, I stated that I had faith in my leader and in his cabinet. I must say that I have now lost that faith. I truly believed that I could trust the Prime Minister of Canada. I said that if he remained at the helm, I would continue to place my confidence in him, but that I would give no blank cheque to any member of the cabinet.
Unfortunately, he is and has been in bad company ever since the demise of that great Canadian, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe who was his mainstay and counsellor. Since then I have seen a change come over our Prime Minister. He is surrounded by conseriptionists and imperialists and is subjected to their influence. This accounts for the fact that less than a fortnight after the plebiscite vote, he unhesitatingly introduced bill 80 which is synonymous with conscription for overseas service.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not dwell further on the matter. I merely wished to express my feelings frankly as is my custom. I was elected on the strength of a certain programme and I have never deceived my electors. As I mentioned earlier in my remarks, I saw in the plebiscite a mask behind which lurked the hideous features of conscription. I was right. At a meeting held prior to the 27th, I stated correctly that two weeks after the plebiscite vote we would have a bill introducing conscription. And that is just what happened.
I cannot close my remarks Mr. Speaker, without congratulating the former Minister of Public Works and of Transport (Mr. Cardin). I am going to speak frankly; I like to be frank. I did not like his speeches on the plebiscite. He is a wonderful speaker, but those of his speeches I heard did not please me; however, he was just as sincere as when he spoke in this house after he had decided to resign from the cabinet. He has devoted his life to politics and represented his race and his province with honour in the commons. There are some who say: "He should have spoken that way before the plebiscite." Perhaps he should have, but it is never too late to mend. There is forgiveness for every sin, and this is even truer in his case because although he was at the head of two government departments he had the courage to resign and to express himself forthrightly in this house. I wish to congratulate him. He is worthy of Ernest Lapointe, he is worthy of all those great French-Canadian Liberals of my province who have sat in this house. He is worthy of Laurier.
His was the crowning gesture of a splendid career. As I was saying a little while ago, I wish those speeches had been made before the plebiscite, but in any event he was sincere. He too had faith in the government. Having been deceived, he had enough courage to resign.
Mr. Speaker, I will not labour the point. Again, I do not beat about the bush; when I want to say something, I come out and say it. I was a member of this house from 1917 to 1925, and have been from 1940 to this day, and each time I have spoken in this parliament I have said what I thought and have said it in French. I have always honoured the French language.
Mr. Speaker, the little calendar that you see' on the table of the house was unilingual when I rose in this house for the first time. If you will look at it now, you will find that it is bilingual. The Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux was then speaker of the house and in the course of a speech I chanced to glance at that calendar. I then asked Mr. Lemieux, who was a patriot, why that little calendar was not bilingual. I told him: "Why don't you have it made bilingual?" Two days later, it was done. Mere details perhaps, yet very important ones from the French Canadian point of view.
When Americans or Englishmen visit the House of Commons and notice this small calendar printed in two languages, they naturally conclude that Canada is a bilingual country. I do not think there is any doubt of it. As I said before, we must uphold the rights granted to us by the constitution, I sat in this house from 1917 to 1925 and I was returned again in 1940. I could speak in English, but as I have the right to speak French I shall continue to do so.
44561-238^

Mobilization Act-Mr. d'Anjou
I remember that in 1924 Mr. Justice Joseph Archambault, then member for Chambly-Vercheres moved a resolution asking that French speeches be translated into English on the day following their utterance in the house. Before then the view was held that French speeches were of very little importance. Practically no one could understand them and they were translated into English some twelve months later. I do not blame my colleagues in this house for speaking English, especially the French Canadian members of the cabinet who must make themselves understood without delay, but if we are to follow the policy of never speaking French in the house solely because some members might not understand us immediately, I wonder what will become of the French tongue in this country. For my part, as long as I enjoy the high honour of representing my constituency, I shall always speak French. Once again, I do not blame my French-Canadian colleagues, and friends, who occasionally speak in English, especially our cabinet ministers. But I have followed a different policy ever since entering the house and I intend to stick to it.
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak at such length. Before concluding I wish to state that I shall never allow any hon. member of this house, irrespective of party, to attack, unchallenged, the province of Quebec. I shall always rise to answer, for I am proud of my constituency and of my province. I conclude by restating my opposition to Bill No. 80. I shall vote against this measure purporting to strike out section 3 of the mobilization act of 1940, which would mean conscription for overseas service.
Mr. DOUGLAS G. ROSS (St. Paul's): Mr. Speaker, this debate has been a long one and there has been a great deal of repetition, but I feel it my duty to say a few words. The house and the country know exactly where I stand on this issue because I made it abundantly clear when I spoke on the plebiscite. One thing that is certain is that when the House of Commons passes this bill it will mean that the government can enforce conscription. There was never any doubt in my mind about the issue at stake in the plebiscite. The plebiscite was introduced for a definite reason, and that reason was whether men should be conscripted for overseas service.
I was opposed to the plebiscite because I felt that the government should have obtained their freedom from parliament. I thought it was putting the cart before the horse, and at that time I said, as reported on page 196 of Hansard:
What do the government hope to gain by a plebiscite? At best the government get a respite
[Mr. d'Anjou.l
of two or three months. Meantime there is all kinds of turmoil. When the three months are up there will be the same pressure for action. This proposal of a plebiscite is an affront to the rights of parliament and an undeserved reflection on the people of this country, of wh itever race or creed, if the proposal carries, it will not get rid of the controversy, and it will leave uncertainty as to future action; if it fails to carry, our troops will be abandoned to the uncertainties of voluntary enlistment. In either case the country is humiliated and disgraced.
How right I was. Before the plebiscite bill passed, there was turmoil in this House of Commons, and since then the country has been disrupted by controversy and recriminations. I said at that time that there was no necessity to split the country in two because parliament could have given the government its freedom. The vote in my riding was a great credit to the sincerity of the people as far as the war effort was concerned. There was no doubt in their minds as to what they were voting on. There was an overwhelming majority in my riding in favour of compulsory service anywhere in the world. The vote was 92-6 per cent "yes", and I think a good many voters voted "no" in the belief that they were going to put the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government on the spot. Otherwise I think the affirmative vote would have been much greater. I should like to pay a tribute to those people who worked so hard in the plebiscite campaign. One thing they had to overcome was what I have just mentioned, the fact that there were so many people, including soldiers, who thought that by voting "no" they could put the Prime Minister and the government on the spot.
I do not like the method we are using to impose conscription. I think we should adopt the method being used in the United States; that is, call men up by lot and give them plenty of time to get ready. The people of the United States are quite proud of their draft army, and no slurs are cast upon the men as is done in this country. I wonder why such slurs are cast on men who are called up? I do not think the selectees in the United States are particularly better fellows; I do not think they are any worse than the members of our volunteer army. I am proud of our volunteer army. I should like to refer briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), and I quote from page 3278 of Hansard as follows:
Who can raise his voice in this house and say that the province of Quebec has been lacking in cooperation with the rest of Canada in every activity, in war as well as in any other line of endeavour? We have been doing our share every moment, in every crisis, in

Mobilization Act-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
every difficult time that confronted Canada. We have measured up to the standard. But we have never been able, even to this moment, to know definitely how many French Canadians have enlisted in English-speaking regiments.
The other day a return was brought down which partly answers the hon. member's question as to how many French Canadians from Quebec have enlisted voluntarily in the army, the navy and the air force. According to this return, 36,235 French Canadians from Quebec have enlisted in the army, the navy and the air force; a total of 29,651 enlisted in the army; 1,474 in the navy, and 5,110 in the air force. That answered his question. Those figures speak for themselves.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: My question was-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
The hon. member can make his speech some other time. I am speaking now.
Again, as reported at page 3277 of Hansard, the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres said:
There is no necessity at the present time to impose such a measure.
Plow does he know that there is no necessity? How does any hon. member know? Why did we take the plebiscite? Why did the three defence ministers rise in their places the other day and speak as they did? Are we to suppose that they did not know what they were talking about? Further on he said:
There is no haste to proceed with such an important measure, which is likely, in the words of the Prime Minister, and in the words of the leader of the opposition as well, to destroy the good understanding which has been established between the two races in Canada for the last forty or fifty years, through troubled hours and difficult days, by the leaders of all parties and those who have taken part in the public life of Canada.
Who has been responsible, I would ask, for the lack of good understanding? Then he went on to say:
Wait for the necessity to arise.
Wait, I suppose, until Hitler is on your doorstep. Let us wait, he says, for the need to present itself. Wait, I suppose, until Hitler comes up the St. Lawrence. The hon. member continued:
Then we shall be in a position to judge according to circumstances what course Canada should follow, what policy Canada should adopt.
I have already pointed to the controversy which has already taken place over conscription, and the hon. member would have us go
through all that again, bring in another bill like this and have hundreds of speeches all over again. That is not reasonable, Mr. Speaker. There is no logic in it.
Wait until the enemy comes up the St. Lawrence river, and then what will happen? If the enemy ever gets up the St. Lawrence river, there will be an uprooting of those roots deeply embedded in the soil of the province of Quebec for 300 years. And not only that; there are other citizens of this country who have roots deeply embedded in the soil, just as much as French Canadians have. We have been in Ontario for a long time, and we do not want our roots uprooted. We think the front line is over there in Britain, and that is where it is.
I wish to quote a few words from the speech of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), who, as reported at page 3413 of Hansard, said:
To come to the armed forces themselves, how could conscription for service overseas help the air force?
It certainly would not hurt it. Some of the draftees could be picked out for the air force. Some of the draftees would apply to go into the air force. That would be all right; it would not hurt the air force. The minister went on:
We could not conscript young men to fly and expect them to be the flyers that we have, fighting in the skies over every battlefront in the world, with no superiors anywhere in the world. No airman can be compelled to fly; he must have the will to do so. It could not be otherwise. The whole of the Royal Air Force is composed of volunteers.
But the air force in the United States is not entirely built up on a voluntary basis. Some of their men have been chosen from the selective service draft, and they do not make such bad flyers. The minister went on to say:
The situation is quite similar with regard to the navy. I am quite certain that the work of the Canadian navy, with its great devotion to duty, with the wonderful record of troop ships convoyed without the loss of a single man, could not have been carried out in the same efficient manner if it had not been done by volunteers.
I think it is marvellous to have a volunteer navy, but there is no reason in the world why a man who was called up under a selective service system could not apply to go into the navy and be accepted. The minister went on:
The only place, therefore, for conscription, if it is of any value at all, is in connection with our army. There, too, I am convinced that it would not make for as effective an army as the Canadian overseas army is at the present time.
3762	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
If these men called up for service anywhere in the world would be no good for the air force, no good for the- navy, and no good for the army overseas, why are they called up for home defence? Is the Minister of National War Services satisfied to have the' men that he is calling up now serving on home defence, to defend our women and children in the case of necessity? I think the minister's remark is a slur on these men who are called up, and I would like to see that slur erased.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) says that we must keep our factories going; that we must keep on producing; that we must have a balanced programme. Certainly we must do that. But does he realize that Great Britain has just called up another 100,000 men from industry, to be drafted into the army, and that these men are to be replaced in industry by women? We still have in this country a great reservoir of potential women workers. And not only that, but if we get down to a proper system of rationing for most of our non-essentials, there will be many more people, men and women, available for work in essential industries. Further -and I draw this to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley)-it might make the bitter pill of increased taxation a little easier to swallow if we had such rationing. If the people could not buy these nonessentials, they would not spend the money and would have it available to pay in taxes.
I was interested in hearing the address given in this house by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght). As reported at page 3632 of Hansard, he said:
We budgeted to increase our forces-the members are all familiar with the details- from 27,000 men now in the navy to 40,000 by March of next year.
Then he went on to say, and I do not quote him fully:
So that the total budget of our man-power by March next is 615,000 men for all the armed forces.
If you are going to budget, you have to find the men to fill your budget, and how are you going to get these men unless you go about it in a proper, businesslike way? These men should be called up two, three, four, five, six, seven or eight months ahead of the time they are required to report. Choose them by lot, and let them know ahead of time when they will be required to report so that they can make their preparations accordingly.
The hon. member for Parry Sound, in criticizing the Military Service Act in force 
in the last war, said, as reported at page 3695 of Hansard:
We were to have 70,000 men by the end of December, 1917, but at the end of March, 1918, we had only 26,000. While the figures show that
61.000	were obtained as a result of that compulsion during the whole period up to armistice day, November 11, during the same period
101.000	men enlisted voluntarily.
But, Mr. Speaker, those 101,000 men who voluntarily enlisted did so under the shadow of conscription. That is what happened.
There is no doubt about it that the front line is overseas, in the fortress of Britain. I should like to quote these words from the Prime Minister's speech, as reported in Hansard, at page 3243:
It is perfectly clear that the enemy will have to be destroyed overseas if this continent is not to be the field of the final conflict, or possibly even an immediate field of conflict, with Canada the scene of the first invasion.
These are potent words. They are the pith picked out of the two-hour pussy-footing speech made by the Prime Minister. Do you believe those words? Let us go to the ministers of national defence for corroboration. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) minced no words in his speech. He said that the result of the plebiscite was an overwhelming mandate for conscription. And then he remarked as reported at page 3509 of Hansard:
A wayfarer plans to journey along a road, and on his map he sees a point where that road branches or forks in two directions. Across one of these branches is an insurmountable barrier, and he says, "When I reach that fork I wish to have freedom to take either branch. Therefore remove the barrier, so that I may have freedom to travel as I think best. I cannot say at this moment which road I shall take. That decision will be made when I reach the junction, and will depend on several factors, some of which are entirely beyond my control."
The minister knows we have reached the barrier, or we shall reach it very shortly, and he is far-sighted enough to see that we cannot afford to wait. We must do our utmost.. We must now take the step.
If you read carefully the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), you will find that he sees the barrier as well. He says that the people of Canada have turned on the green light to go ahead with this bill, under the mandate they have given the government for conscription for overseas.
I come now to the magnificent speech made by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). All one has to do is to read it to know he has seen the barrier ahead and wishes to take the step at the present time. Opposed, as he has always been, to conscription, would he have taken the step which he took in the house last week, after his family

Mobilization Act-^Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
had represented Quebec South for forty years, with all the sentiment which was attached to it between himself and his constituents, unless he had thought such a step was necessary? No, Mr. Speaker. I compliment the hon. gentleman upon the course he took in this house the other day. When it comes to the time of the next election his electors will probably think pretty well of him. He says he is first a Canadian and then a Quebecker. I am first a Canadian, and after that I am an Ontarian. We must all be Canadians in that sense, in these days, if we are to lick the Hun.
I come to the speech of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard). He said that he would have voted for the bill had it not been for past history. He complained bitterly about the lack of political education with an eye to overcoming the prejudices between the various provinces of Canada. He said he could not educate his constituents in a week. Certainly he could not. And whose fault was that? That of the political leaders of the province of Quebec who in the past have raised these issues at every election which has been held. Why have they done this? The political leaders in Quebec have for years been making political capital out of these issues in order to hold the balance of power in Canadian politics. This has been on many occasions their avowed intention. Is there any wonder that the policy pursued by them is resented in the other provinces? Until that situation is cleared up, we shall never have national unity.
With respect to the measure before us, I submit that the time has come when opposition must cease. Canada's future is at stake. The future of the British commonwealth of nations is imperilled. The eyes of the world are on us at the present time.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Before the six o'clock recess I had said that Canada's needs at the present time were greater than those of any province. I might point out what tremendous significance there is in the words of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) when he said in effect that he is for national unity, but unity cannot stand in the way of Canada's safety, and Canada is in peril.
The other day the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) quoted some speeches from the British House of Commons of January, 1916, with reference to the debate on the military service bill. He quoted statements in
support of one side of the picture; he quoted the then Prime Minister (Mr. Asquith). That Prime Minister, as we all know, was a great prime minister, but he was a peace-time prime minister and his great forte was compromise. He did not quote anyone on the other side. I wish to take this opportunity of quoting a few words spoken by the then Secretary of State for the Colonies, Mr. Bonar Law, which express my own opinion better than I could do myself. He said, as reported in British Hansard for 1915-16, January 5, 1916, page 1010:
When this war broke out I felt as strongly as those who had taken the most active part in what is called the national service movement, that our method of raising recruits by the voluntary system was not a good method for such a war as this. I thought it was not a good method, first of all, because it seemed to me utterly unfair that in the same town, or perhaps in the same street, three or four sons of one family should go, and another family on whom the state had precisely the same claim should not send a single man to the army.
I agree with that. I also think that the privilege of citizenship carries with it the duty of defence of one's country.
Mr. Bonar Law said further:
I thought it a bad system for another reason, the very reason on which many of those who are opposed to this bill oppose it now-that it was a wasteful system, and that if we were to make any attempt to have a proper correlation between the men employed in the necessary civil services and those who go to fight our battles, that could not be arrived at by a system of haphazard enlistment and recruiting which depended on the voluntary will of individual people.
What about that situation? Why did it become acute? As I said this afternoon, the barrier which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) spoke about was in sight. What actually had been happening at that time was that recruiting had fallen off; they said that it was going to be worse and that they had to take wounded men who had come back to England for convalescence and send them to the front two and three times and the public became incensed.
What is wrong with compulsory selective service? Why is it not right? I cannot see any reason why it is not. Drawing your selectees by lot is a pretty fair way of doing it. Let us take a look across the border; how does it work there? They are proud of their selectees; they cannot do enough for them. They are called up in the regular way, given plenty of time so that they can make their arrangements before they join the army. That is the method we should adopt in this country.
What is the position of a young man in Canada to-day? He has a very difficult decision to make. Many of them do not know
3764	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
whether they are doing their duty or not. Should they finish their university course; should they still be working in the factories; is it fair that they should have to make this choice themselves? How can they make the choice, when there seems to be such a divided opinion in the cabinet itself? Surely the ministers know the situation; there should not be any division in the cabinet in that respect. What a conglomeration of ideas we have had from the ministry, with the exception of the three ministers of national defence!
Are the other ministers real, honest-to-goodness Canadians, or are they politicians? Why have this division in the cabinet when the facts are known to the minister? Why not let us have some real, fearless leadership, as shown by the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, and the Minister of National Defence for Air? I cannot pay too high tribute to the latter minister for the way he handled the situation with which he is faced in this house. Let us get rid of the slurs cast at our conscripts; let us call them up by lot. Life is a gamble anyway. Most people are good gamblers; when they are called up by lot they will take their chances like everyone else; they will be tickled to death, in fact, if they know what they have to do.
This debate started some weeks ago, and it seems likely to continue for some time yet. Let me make a suggestion. We have had a tremendous amount of repetition of ideas of one kind and another, and no doubt there are many more hon. members who want to speak in the debate. I suggest they be allowed to prepare a speech, write it and have it placed on Hansard, and they will thus get themselves on record. I think it is a good suggestion, for the same things are being repeated over and over. I am probably doing the same thing; I doubt very much whether 1 have contributed anything new to the debate.
What are our obligations? We are obligated not only to the defence of our own country, but to the defence of Great Britain, the united nations, the Chinese, the Russians. If there was ever any time when Canada should show herself in the best light and come to the help of the gallant Russian people who have held the foe back all this time, it is now. Where should we be but for them? We know we must open a second front; we must get the men for that, and we must keep our factories going. We cannot let our armies overseas and our navy and our air force down when that second front is opened.
I have just one last word to offer. I hope I have not offended anyone in what I have said to-day. I have spoken from the bottom of 
my heart; I have said what I thought. I appeal for unity to carry out the will of the people as expressed during the plebiscite recently held. Let us all fight together, Mr. Speaker, or they will kill us one by one.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I am indeed fortunate to-might, Mr. Speaker. The first time I had the privilege of speaking in this house I followed my good friend the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross), who has again preceded me in this debate. With one thing that he said I must agree, and I am not being personal at all. He said he wondered what some of the preceding speakers had contributed to the debate. I also wonder. Some of my political opponents took what I consider to be an unfair advantage of me, though they may consider it fair political strategy. Last Friday I was invited to be the ninth member of a baseball team made up by my good friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and Social Credit parties to play a team of House of Commons pages. I do not know why I was asked to be the ninth member of that team, unless it was because they could not muster nine players from the two groups, and so I, the most radical member of the other parties, was asked to complete the team. I had the privilege of playing in the outfield, along with my good friend the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). He and I, coming from the Pacific coast, talk a good game of baseball ; that is, our chatter is good though our playing is not. We both talked our heads off, and as a result I am hoarse to-night. The hon. member for Vancouver East need not care, because he does not have to speak. Then they placed me in centre field, where I had to back up a member of the Social Credit party at second base. He neither caught nor stopped one ball, and of course I had to chase the ball until I was stiff, but in spite of it all the umpire saw to it that we won the game. Then my good friends the Conservatives, perhaps trying to put me at a disadvantage, taking advantage of the preparations being made outside for some coming ceremony, told me that I was not to speak to-night but that the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) and I were to have a joint debate on the platform being erected outside the building, and I waited there for twenty minutes. Incidentally, I had better watch the clock, because I believe the time is being checked very closely.
I would not be addressing the house to-night, Mr. Speaker, but for the fact that I consider it the duty of every member of this house who is a returned soldier to express his views in connection with this bill; his duty not only

Mobilization Act-Mr. Cruickshank
to the veterans of the last war but also to the veterans of this war. Before I have concluded my remarks I hope to make quite clear how I stand in connection with the vote that is to be taken shortly. I might mention that we in this corner of the house, commonly known as the "Rump", are very proud of the fact that seven of our members are serving in the active forces; that six of our members are veterans of the last war, and that many of those in our corner have sons serving in this war.
In passing, I might mention that I intend placing on the order paper a question asking what members of this house are veterans of the last war, what members are serving in this war, and what members have sons serving.
I am asking that question for a reason which was particularly emphasized by the speech of one hon. member this afternoon. I want to bring to the attention of the people of Canada the fact that many members of this house either are serving to-day or have sons serving.
I wish to do that for this reason. Who would have more sympathy, more respect, and a greater desire to help our soldiers overseas in every way possible, than those who are serving themselves or who have sons serving? To-day one hon. member was asked whether he was entirely in sympathy with this bill or any other bill having to do with the welfare of Canada and of our soldiers. That hon. member has a son who is perhaps flying over Germany to-night, and I think I am entitled to bring that fact to the attention of the people of Canada, as I intend to do.
Just here I should like to pay my respects to what I consider the most courageous speech ever made in this House of Commons, or at least since I have been a member of it. I refer to the speech made by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). No one questions the great value of the work he did as the organizing genius behind our greatest contribution to the allied cause, the commonwealth air training scheme. The minister suggested that because of the stand he is taking at the present time it may be necessary for him to sacrifice his seat.
