subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I am only repeating what the minister said. I want to state, on behalf of British Columbia, that should that time ever come my seat will be available to the minister, and I think I am safe in saying that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and Conservative members of this house will help me to see that the minister is elected unanimously. In this connection I would also mention the hon. member for
Wright (Mr. Leduc), a private member, it is quite true, but one whose courage should be recognized. I should like to quote one or two paragraphs from his remarks, and I am only sorry that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) is not present. I am not a wealthy man, but I hope the hon. member for Parkdale will see to it that his famous committee of 200, which includes the wealthiest men in Canada, will have the speech of the hon. member for Wright printed and distributed to every elector in the province of Quebec. As reported at page 3729 of Hansard for June 26 the hon. member for Wright said:
I am well aware that such a stand will prejudice my chances of reelection to this house; but, faced with the choice of serving my country or being reelected, I do not hesitate in choosing to serve my country.
And again:
I ask nothing more than to have my supporters and fellow citizens of the province of Quebec understand that our soldiers overseas are defending both England and Canada; that our airmen, striking formidable blows at the enemy in Europe, are defending Canada; that our sailors who seek out the enemy on our coasts and on the high seas are also defending Canada. I trust that, once and for all, my fellow citizens of Quebec and elsewhere-[DOT]
I should like to emphasize the words "and elsewhere."
-in Canada will realize that this is not England's war, but a war being waged by Great Britain, Canada and all the united nations in the defence of our liberties and our Christian civilization.
I could go on quoting from that great speech, but time does not permit.
In my own riding all three parties combined and worked with all the other organizations, and particularly the Canadian Legion, in an endeavour to secure a most emphatic "yes" vote. We were successful to the approximate extent of 80 per cent. I am not in a position to say that an 80 per cent vote was a vote for conscription immediately, in the near future, or at any time. But I am in a position to say most emphatically on behalf of my riding that the people there believe in total war. In our minds total war means exactly what it says; it means conscription of every kind, be it wealth, man-power or industry.
I must admit frankly that I prepared certain notes for this speech. Perhaps I made a mistake in doing this. A speech I could have made, one which would have been most effective, would have been a presentation of newspaper headlines collected throughout the world in the last two years. To-night's headline points out that the fall of Matruh is officially confirmed. I do not believe it is necessary for me to turn to my notes in that
3766	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Cruickshank
connection to say what people in British Columbia, and most certainly those in Fraser Valley, feel at this time. We believe there is nothing any member of the house or any individual in Canada can do that is enough under the present trying and serious conditions.
I am proud that since the beginning of the war and, in fact, before the war, speaking as a returned soldier, I have preached or advocated what I believed was a proper policy for Canada. I believe, and always will believe in a policy of compulsory selective service, and it is in that policy that my constituency believes. I do not know if they believe in immediate conscription of man-power, but I do know they are behind the policy of compulsory selective service. As I understand it, they realize the seriousness of the situation, and it is possible that we of the Fraser Valley are in a better position than many in that respect. In common with a few-a very few- other members, some from British Columbia, I was scoffed at when I pointed out the seriousness of the Japanese situation. I was scoffed at when I said that every battle which has been lost in this war to date has been lost, not through lack of man-power but through lack of mechanical equipment and through organized fifth column activity. What would have happened to British Columbia if we had been complacent, and, through our silence, had permitted 20,000 fifth-columnist Japanese to remain in our province?
I am pointing that out for this reason: while I may disagree with government policy in some instances, would I be a true Canadian or a true Britisher if, because of that disagreement with past or present policy, I voted against the bill? I do not think so, and I do not believe my hon. friends from Quebec think so. We believe in total war-war with no restrictions. No pledges can prevent us from carrying out our duties as we see them as Canadians and members of the British empire. We believe the war must be fought to every extreme; we must meet the enemy at every angle, and, if possible, be on the initiative in meeting him.
In that connection may I refer to one of the greatest patriots of our sister nation, Joe Louis. He happens to be a coloured man, but he is serving willingly in the army of his country. He is serving voluntarily under a proper selective system. Furthermore, on many occasions he has given voluntarily, in a financial way, through benefits on behalf of the services, more than any other individual of whom I know serving in any allied army. Would Joe Louis ever have become the great victor he is in his own line of endeavour if he 
had waited for the enemy to attack? Of course not. No other great fighter ever became a victor in that way. The secret of his reputation and his victorious career has been that he has carried the battle to his opponents.
If your neighbour's roof is on fire, would you wait until that fire spread through your own woodshed before attempting to put it out? Would you not attempt to assist in putting it out while it is still on your neighbour's roof? The answer is obvious.
The proper way to meet modern warfare methods is to combat them with the antidotes of those methods. Methods of warfare must be met with an absolute understanding of what those methods mean. In my view- and I state this frankly-in so far as it concerns man-power for overseas I believe the importance of conscription has been overexaggerated. I do not know if conscription is needed to-day, or if it will be needed to-morrow or the next day to keep our army up to full strength. There are only three men who know that, namely, the three ministers of the defence services.
I have always been in favour of national selective service; but whether it is necessary to-day or to-morrow, I do not know. Certainly I cannot understand some of my friends in the Conservative party and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I want to be fair to them by stating that both those parties worked, and worked hard, to secure a "yes" vote in my riding. In its programme fhe Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has said, "No conscription of manpower unless we have conscription of wealth". The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) recently before a convention of the greatest organization in Canada-the Canadian Legion-said that he believed in the conscription of wealth before the enforcement of any other kind of conscription. That, at least, is my understanding of what he said.
I agree entirely with that, and have so stated on many occasions. I believe manpower should be conscripted, and, speaking as a veteran of the last war, I believe in the conscription of wealth. But I would say to my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation:	If this new budget
does not carry with it conscription of wealth, then all I can say is that I have a railway ticket which will take me back home, but I will need some Social Credit money to pay for my meals on the train. I appeal to them on the ground that we now have conscription of wealth to vote for Bill No. 80 when it comes to a vote on the second reading. If

Mobilization Act-Mr. Cruickshank
they sincerely believe in the conscription of wealth, then I say they have received almost all they asked for.
At this time I should like to read a short paragraph from a United States newspaper. Of course this does not apply to the member for Fraser Valley, but would apply to some other hon. members. This quotation from the San Francisco Argonaut, bearing the heading "Candid Opinion", states:
If somebody were to establish an endowment fund to award prizes for stupidity we strongly suspect that the greater number of awards would go to members of our congress. It almost makes a man lose his faith in democracy when he sees the kind of human jackasses that get elected to our halls of legislation to make laws for us.
That is from a United States paper. Why do not many members of the House of Commons and Canadians in general, instead of criticizing our war effort at all times, instead of trying to change our great national outdoor game of lacrosse to a mutual indoor game of knocking our Prime Minister and knocking our war effort, adopt the policy of one of the greatest leaders ever developed, particularly in war time, Mr. Wendell Willkie? They should paraphrase his statement and say, "He is my prime minister; Canada is at war; I am a Canadian." Mistakes and errors have been made, but is there any government at war to-day that has not made errors? Why should not the members of this house and the people of Canada tell with pride of our production of tanks, ships, munitions of war and food? As a member of parliament I have had the privilege of seeing that production, as have all members. Is there any greater assistance that we can give to the skunk of all skunks, Hitler; to the runt of all runts, Mussolini, to the scab of all scabs, Hirohito, than to criticize Canada's war effort?
Mistakes have been made in the past, and we are going to make them again. I do not want the house to think I am condoning all the mistakes the government has made. In my opinion the greatest mistake the government has made in the face of our need for conscription has been what I referred to a year ago, the utter stupidity of our recruiting campaign. I happen to be a supporter of the government, but I blame them for our recruiting campaign. One thing that I hold against the government is that they have endeavoured too often to pass on the mistakes we have made. I should like to quote briefly from some of the statements I made to my electors when I was requesting a "yes" vote in the plebiscite. I quote these for the simple reason that I want there to be no mistake about where I stand. I am a member of the
Liberal party, a supporter of the Liberal party. I am a British Columbian and I am a Canadian, but above all I am a Britisher. Being a Britisher is above being a Canadian, being a British Columbian or being a member of any political party. The'statements I intend to quote appeared in the press of my riding. This may be a small country press, but I do not think it needs to apologize to the press of any province or of any riding in Canada. I quote:
It is to be hoped every one will make the forthcoming plebiscite their own personal problem, will consider the future conduct of our war effort as their own responsibility and say to the government by an overwhelming affirmative vote, "you now have a free hand, no obstacles of any kind in the prosecution of the war to the very extent of Canada's ability to produce the materials of war, either in wealth, industry or man-power; we, the people, demand an entire and all-out war effort and will support all and any action necessary to bring victory."
I am quoting this to show where I stood, and I think I speak with authority for my riding. I quote again:
In particular I urge and every individual and organization who have called for total war now put that just call in practice in a practical way open to all, by seeing that an overwhelming "yes" vote is recorded in the valley on the 27th of April.
One more paragraph in that connection:
It can happen here, it most likely will happen here;
That was said in April and since then there have been two attacks on the Pacific coast and a ship has been sunk off Vancouver island. I quote:
We have no time for complacency by governments, we most certainly have no time for complacency by individuals. One it may be hard to control, can it be said it is hard to control our own actions? Let us all ask ourselves not what the other fellow' is doing to defend us from bombs, hit and run attacks, or vrar in any of its horrible forms, but instead ask ourselves the simple question, w'hat am I doing to protect my very own home and family and the families of those away offering their lives to protect us, we all have a duty.
That is what I wrote in connection with the plebiscite.
I should like to say a word or two about Quebec. I think most of the Quebec members are personal friends of mine. Most of them endeavoured to secure an affirmative vote in the plebiscite. I appreciate their problem because in many cases an affirmative vote was not secured. I realize that their political future may be at stake should they vote "yes" on this amending bill. There was an 80 per cent affirmative vote in my riding. I want to ask my hon. friends from Quebec: What will

Mobilization Act-Mr. Cruickshank
happen to your conscience if the time should come-and it will come sooner or later-I am very much afraid it will come very soon- when our troops will cry for trained reinforcements? If you advocated a "yes" vote in the plebiscite in order to relieve the government of every obligation, why not be consistent and vote "yes" now? Why not trust your government ; why not trust your leader that conscription will be put in force when and if necessary? Why not realize that if you can advocate a "yes" vote when times are not so serious, you should maintain that stand by voting "yes" now?
What are you going to say to the rest of the provinces if the British isles are invaded? If the British isles are invaded, Canada's Pacific and Atlantic coasts will be invaded. What are you going to say to the people who said in 1885, "Our hearts belong to France but our arms belong to England?" My friends, your hearts may belong to France, but the mother country of France is a conquered country today, and she will remain conquered unless your arms are given to the empire to relieve her. Make no mistake about that. I should like to repeat a statement I heard over the radio on Sunday in connection with the United States war effort. I think it is extremely apropos to the present position. I am speaking particularly to my hon. friends from Quebec, and I want to assure them that I would have been in just as difficult a position had my riding voted "no." Let me say to them: You may have a temporary gain, but the empire means more than you or I as political individuals. This -was a programme in connection with the war effort of the United States and the theme was, "Eternity is a long time for a man to be ashamed."
I have every confidence in and every admiration for members from the province of Quebec. They have a difficult problem. I, too, might have a difficult problem to explain to my riding. Frankly, many people in my riding might consider it my duty as a Canadian from British Columbia to condemn the attitude of the province of Quebec, but I do not believe that is what the people of Canada want. Of course, we all become more tolerant as we grow older, but I do not think it should necessarily be compulsory to put any young man into a uniform. I do not claim particularly to be a young man, but still I am rather ashamed of the fact that I am not in uniform to-day. I do not have a son, but if I happened to have a son he would not have to be forced by law to get into uniform. If he did not join the army of his own accord, I would shoot him myself. That is what I think of the British empire.

We are sitting here dawdling around in complacency, both individuals and the government, and we do not know there is a war on. We are stalling. Read the headlines in to-day's papers and the headlines of yesterday and the day before. Are we ever going to wake up-not as members of parliament or as a government but as citizens of Canada? There is a war on. We are not fighting to protect the British empire or to protect Canada; we are fighting to protect our very existence-make no mistake about that.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope that I have offended no one, particularly anyone from the province of Quebec, by my remarks, but I thought it my duty as a returned soldier member to speak on this question. I am somewhat surprised that other than returned soldier members have spoken in this debate. It is not necessary to have any bitterness, but I do think it is necessary that we as Canadians should remember that we would not be Canadians sitting here to-night if it were not for the great traditions and the actions of the British navy.
I am an infantry man and an army man myself, but before I sit down I should like to quote two stanzas of a poem by one of our gallant airmen, Squadron Leader G. L. Creed, entitled "Somebody's Son"; but just before doing so, let me say to my good friends from Quebec and from every other province, in every district and every riding, let us have no illusions that we would have the privilege of sitting here and speaking to-night if it were not for Britain and the British navy:
Somebody's son has volunteered To risk his life for you,
Somebody's son is far from home And the things that homefolk do.
Somebody's son for your freedom's sake Is preparing himself for war,
Somebody's son deserves your help For it's You he is fighting for!
Somebody's mother is giving her boy In a cause that is yours as well.
Somebody's wife knows a loneliness That only her heart can tell.
Somebody's mother and somebody's wife Are doing all they can do.
Somebody prays that some other may care. And the answer is up to You!
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops):	Mr. Speaker, I feel very much honoured in following the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), but I hope he will pardon me if I do not follow along exactly the same lines that he took. I do not take up very much of the time of the house and probably would not be speaking to-night if it were not for the fact that some speeches have been made in this debate which make it almost impossible for a man to continue to sit

Mobilization Act-Mr. O'Neill
silent. I do not think I can add anything new to what has already been said. I doubt, indeed, whether very much more can be said, but I think we should give some consideration to the reason for this legislation. The reason for this legislation is quite a long story, but there are some events of quite recent occurrence to which we might well give consideration at this time.
Some of the members on the opposite side of the house, and particularly of the Conservative party, seem to have the idea that politics, and particularly Liberal party politics, is a crime, at least at this time, although Conservative party politics has certainly been intensified both in this house and through the press under the guise of National government.
I think we are all fairly well agreed that we must have some sort of party government and political parties if democratic government is to function. There must be a party in power, and a party in opposition. As long as I have known anything about politics, I have been taught that the best form of government is one with a strong working majority, faced by a strong opposition. The advocates of National government are advocating exactly the reverse. They would take all the able men out of the opposition and put them in the government. The result would be that we would have a much more powerful government and a much weaker opposition. If the theory is sound that we should have a government with a strong working majority, and a strong opposition, then surely in a time of crisis we should not attempt to make a government weaker by putting more strength into it at the expense of a strong opposition.
As far back as July, 1939, when I returned to this country from Geneva, I found that the Conservative party had started on a campaign to elect a National government. The then leader of the Conservative party was making a tour of the Gaspe peninsula in the interests of the Conservative party, under the guise of a National government, which at that time they were advocating. Later on, in 1940, the election was fought on two distinct issues: one of them was national government versus party government, the other was, as was most emphatically affirmed by all three major parties, no conscription for overseas service. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), was elected in that year with the greatest majority received by any man at any time in the history of this country. Ever since that election the Conservative party and the Conservative press have done everything humanly possible to destroy Mr. King politically, and his government, and to set up in their stead a National government. As as example
of how far things have gone along that line, let me quote what a professor named C. W. Topping, of the university of British Columbia, said before the League of Nations Society of Canada convention recently held in Ottawa:
His students do not find much sense in fighting for the status quo. The Conservatives have made too good a job in tearing down Mackenzie King.
That was said at a League of Nations Society meeting on May 30, 1942. It is not a party matter. Toronto Saturday Night, which I submit is not a Liberal newspaper, had this to say:
Conscriptionists killing conscription.
Further on:
Mr. King is clever.
And still further:
Our regret at Mr. King's course has a different basis. The political insiders may view these things in the manner that we have surmised; but the public does not. The public of the eight provinces has been worked up into the belief that conscription is "necessary," though With no very definite idea for what reasons or by what standards; into a belief that it voted for the enactment and enforcement of conscription; and into a consequent feeling that conscription ought to be enacted and enforced. The present parliamentary debates and press editorials do not fully represent its reaction. It is disillusioned and disappointed. It has come to regard conscription as the "just" way of raising a large military force, and any other way as unjust to certain classes and detrimental to the future character of the nation.
That is something which has been raised up in the minds of the people through the debates in this house and by editorials throughout this country for the past five months. We have been here since last January, and I submit that this house has done nothing but talk conscription pro and con, either on the plebiscite or during the debate which is now proceeding.
The question before parliament to-day is the repeal of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act. As the natural consequence of the plebiscite, and the plebiscite, in my opinion, was the only fair, logical and democratic thing to do under the circumstances. The people of the constituency of Kamloops, which I have the honour to represent, did not vote "yes" on the plebiscite in the belief that it was a vote for conscription at once. I believe they had enough intelligence, knowing that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell), and the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Mackenzie King), on the public platform, over the air and through the newspapers told them most emphatically that an
Mobilization Act-Mr. O'Neill

affirmative vote was not a vote for conscription, to understand that they were not voting for conscription, but they certainly did know that if they voted "no" the hands of the government of this country would remain tied. They wanted to release the hands of the government so that they would be prepared at any time to take the action which in their best judgment seemed to be the right action to take at the time. It was not intended, as some people suggest, that we should blindly drive into conscription even though it were not necessary in order to win the war. That may appeal to the ideas of some people, but it was not what actuated the people of my constituency in voting "yes" -which they did, in unmistakable terms.
As I understand it, there are sufficient powers in the mobilization act to mobilize and conscript everything in this country, including man-power, except that the government must not conscript men for service overseas. This bill is the natural and logical result of the plebiscite, its intention being to remove that restriction. Not that we must put conscription into effect to-morrow, but conscription is to be introduced if and when in the opinion of the governing body of this country it is necessary. The government, I submit, are the only people who have the necessary information to decide that matter.
What is the record and what are the policies of those who are opposed to the government? I will begin with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. May I at the outset pay tribute to the leader of that party in respect of the exceedingly able and well-delivered proposals of his party. May I also tell him that with some of his submissions, especially those having reference to the three guiding rules of the New Zealand labour government as laid down by the Hon. Walter Nash, I am in complete agreement. But I am somewhat at a loss to reconcile the present attitude of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation with some of its past utterances and performances. On June 11, when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was making his presentation to the house, he is credited in Hansard, at page 3262, with the following language:
We of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have always contended that the financial system should be publicly owned and operated for the common good.
May I say at once that I am in complete agreement with that expression. But that has not always been the position of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. In 1934, before I had the honour and privilege 
of being a member of this house there was instituted in this country the Bank of Canada. The bill constituting this bank was brought in by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who at that time was Prime Minister, and the majority of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party of that day voted with the government for private ownership of that bank. I point that out merely to call attention to the fact that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation of that time were not of the same opinion as that now expressed by the leader of that group, who himself was not a member at that time; he came in, as I did, at the election of 1935.

Would the hon. member
allow me to say-
Mr. O'NEILL: I have sat here for months and months and listened to many speeches from the hon. member. I have only a little time at my disposal.

I want to correct
the hon. member's statement. His assertions are wrong. There was no Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this house in 1934.
Mr. O'NEILL: No; the party came into being in 1932; none of you were elected as Cooperative Commonwealth Federation representatives, but you held the same sort of views as you hold now; you have adapted them to the times.
