speechtext:
We will tell you later about the screwball amendment against which we voted.
Mr. O'NEILL: I have not interrupted the hon. member since 1935. I assure him there were plenty of times that I should like to have interrupted him with an ink bottle, but I let him go on, and I think he might do the same with me now. I might call attention to the fact that the hon. member who has seen fit to interrupt me voted with the Conservative government for private ownership of the Bank of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
That is not true.
Mr. O'NEILL: Look at the record.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I say it is not true.
Mr. O'NEILL: Look at the record and you will see it is true.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
That is not true.
Mr. O'NEILL: The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party went on to say, as reported at page 3262 of Hansard:
Hon. members will have noticed that one of the first controls which the government found it necessary to impose in this war was the control of foreign exchange. Banks are instru

Mobilization Act-Mr. O'Neill
ments of financial and investment policy. _ It is absurd to leave any portion of the policy in private hands during a crisis such as the present.
With that last remark I am in accord. However, I might point out that in the election of 1940 the only man who advocated from a public platform that there should be conscription of wealth, industry and manpower was the Hon. W. D. Herridge, who was defeated in the constituency' of Kindersley. But now we have many followers of that doctrine.
Let me now discuss the stand of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation on former occasions. There was quite a little argument the other night in respect of socialism. As I understand it-I am open to correction if I am wrong-I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) put forth the aims and objects of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation on that occasion, and I believe he was contending that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are not socialists. I might call the attention of hon. members to the fact that in the Regina Leader-Post of June 18 there was this notice:
The C.C.F. will hold a leadership school at Crystal Lake in the Canora district from July 6 to 11, at which members of parliament, members of the legislative assembly, candidates, members of the provincial council and campaign managers and organizers will be present. Guest speaker will be J. W. Bunee, Professor of Economics, at Iowa State College, who will instruct in the economics of socialism.
Mind you, I have no quarrel with the principles of socialism. What I have quarrelled with is the methods that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation seek to apply. We go back to 1936 and find this. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had this to say on May 28, as reported at page 3203 of Hansard of that year:
.	.	. in my opinion a country the size of
Canada, with its divers peoples and small population, is best defended if we rely upon our weakness physically and our goodwill as a good world neighbour rather than attempt to ape the military powers of the European countries.
I contend that is not a very laudable sentiment to be expressed by a man who seeks to be a leader of a great party. Then on November 15, 1937, he said, as reported at page 888 of Hansard of that year:
Are we in Canada going to join in this mad race without knowing precisely the policy that underlies the increased estimates upon which we shall shortly have to vote? Our answer in this little group is, of course, no, because we believe that such defence preparations only breed fear and that hate, which, in turn, is the child of fear.
Then on February 22, 1937, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, as reported at page 1102 of Hansard of that year:
We have to bear in mind that in any war we should be involved largely on account of our association with some other country. It might be because of proximity to the United States, or because of our connection with Great Britain, even if we declared neutrality. We must remember that either of those nations has a navy powerful enough to prevent the passage of aircraft carriers across the Atlantic, and would be prepared to stop them for their own protection and the protection of their trade routes.
That is the party which to-day tells us that the Liberal party is not going far enough.
Again on February 22, 1937, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, as reported at page 1105 of Hansard of that year:
If we once put our feet along this path of providing gun emplacements, coastal defences and so on, we must realize that we may be led much farther than we are given to understand to-day we will be. I am thoroughly convinced of that, and that is one reason why I am opposing this estimate. I believe that with a coast line such as we have, to do as the government intends will mean embarking upon a course which will be more or less provocative and interfere with any neutrality we may desire to observe in the future.
About the same time, May 8, 1936, the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) said, as reported at page 2632 of Hansard of that year:
When it comes to voting money for these purposes I desire to register a protest, not because I think these things are unnecessary, but because I think there are other things that are more necessary.
On February 19, 1937, the hon. member for Weyburn said, as reported at page 1063 of Hansard of that year:
Against whom are we arming? Wliat potential aggressor, is more agressive to-day? Oh I know that bogeymen have been trotted out in this chamber. It has been suggested that it might be Italy, it might be Germany, it might be Japan.
I suggest that if the hon. member had been a prophet instead of a critic in that day he would have been a world-beater.
Speaking on the plebiscite, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had this to say:
I welcomed the opportunity to speak to you to-night-not only to urge you to vote "yes" next Monday, which I do, but also fo outline to you my views, and those of the movement for which I speak, on the whole picture of our war effort and Canada's hopes for the future.
I might remark that this is the only time I ever knew any government to pay for spreading political propaganda of their opponents.
With respect to our friends of the Conservative party, we have heard a good deal from

Mobilization Act-Mr. O'Neill
our friends with respect to leadership. Most of those remarks I believe emanated from the leaderless league in Toronto. They have indicated that they have no leadership, but they constantly advocated that the Prime Minister should get out and that someone else should get in; they asked for total war and so on. To my mind, remarks and tactics of that kind cannot have any other effect than to undermine the confidence of the people of this country in democratic government. I care not who is in power, whether Liberals or Conservatives, tactics of that kind by the opposition can have no other effect. It is my opinion that that very thing was more responsible for the fall of France than anything else. That went on in France until the country fell.
We heard this afternoon the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the other night the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) talking about the ballot box. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have not heard any members of the Liberal party talk about the ballot box. Those remarks came from the opposition; and it was the wrong construction they placed on the utterances of those who preceded them in this debate that led them to accuse men of placing the ballot box before the good of their country. We could all go on doing these things, calling each other names, but it would not help the situation one iota. Hon. members who make remarks of that kind, however, would be surprised at what some uncharitable people might say about them as a consequence.
I submit that our war effort has been admirable in the eyes of all throughout the world with the exception of those in this country who are opposed to this government. They are the people who are doing everything humanly possible to belittle and discredit Canada's effort in this struggle for freedom. Hon. Walter Nash, who is now New Zealand's representative in the United States and who was formerly Minister of Finance of New Zealand, in addressing a special committee of this house had this to say:
We have sent . . . men overseas and . . . of these are airmen who have a lot of skill and knowledge as a rtsult of the training they have received under the magnificent empire air training scheme which you are carrying out here in Canada. If that alone was Canada's contribution with respect to this war it is something to be particularly proud of.
That is only one of the many things Canada is doing in this war; but this gentleman, who leans very far to the left as far as politics are concerned, considers that if it were the only thing, still our effort would be magnificent.
I am sure we all listened with a great deal of interest when the Minister of Munitions
[Mr. O'Neill.!
and Supply (Mr. Howe) told us what the government was doing in the. way of furnishing supplies to the allied nations. If my memory serves me correctly without referring to Hansard, we were told by the minister that munitions and war equipment manufactured in Canada were seeing service on every fighting front in the world to-day. We wrere also told that the tanks we are sending to Russia are among the finest in the world.
At this time I should like to congratulate the government upon what they have done in the way of putting representatives of labour on various boards, and upon having chosen a real labour man to head that department. When I say he is a real labour man, I expect the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation will, of course, not agree. I say these things, Mr. Speaker, because we are constantly told that we must conscript men for overseas service.
This is a news item which I clipped from the Ottawa Citizen of June 17. It comes from Vancouver, one of the finest cities in north America, and states:
C. S. Henley, special representative here for the national selective service board, announced to-day that labour shortages in British Columbia s vital spruce camps had been filled by soldier-loggers given six months leave from the torces, and that a similar plan to fill labour gaps in war industries was in the tentative stage.
Mr. Henley said that the soldiers were sent to spruce camps, chiefly in the Queen Charlotte islands, about three weeks ago.
I mention that in passing because we are told that we must have conscription for overseas service at once, whether or not men are required for other war work. I might read one other clipping along the same line, from the Monetary Times of June 20:
Faced with an acute labour shortage . farmers of the Fraser vallev in British Columbia have appealed to Colonel A. W. Sparling, D.S.O., local army commander, to release soldiers for work on the farms.
The head of one of the associations making the appeal said:
The men could be released to work on the farms on an eight-hour day basis at wages arranged by the military authorities.
I was pleased to note the appointment of Mr. E. M. Little to the selective service board. In speaking to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Mr. Little had this to say:
Employer-employee relations can and must be improved. Without them, maximum efficiency cannot exist. With good relations, miracles can be performed. There are men in this room who have been leaders in establishing sound relations with their employees. There are some who would like to have good relations and don't know how to go about it. And there are some employees who don't seem to want good relations.

Mobilization Act-Mr. O'Neill
To those who are willing, but don't know how, will you find out how from those who do? To those who don't want good relations or don't appreciate their value, I say the country cannot afford to have you as an employer at any time, particularly in war time. You must change your ways.
I suggest that if we had more of that sentiment we might be able to increase our war effort quite considerably. A Hamilton labour leader, Mr. John Mitchell, had this to say along the same line:
Employers who refuse to cooperate with their workers are a menace. They are breeders of discontent, hatred .and spite, and kill the initiative of the workers.
I think on the whole it can be said without fear of successful contradiction that while the government of this country has made many mistakes, when the history of these times is written, the record of this country will be among the most glorious of all of those who have taken part in this struggle for freedom. The present relations existing between Great Britain, our splendid neighbour the United States, and Canada, can in all fairness I think, be attributed to the statesmanship of our present Prime Minister. No one in this country, even those newspapers which are most strongly against the Prime Minister and his government, ever says anything against the ministers in charge of our war effort: the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), ;he Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), and the Minister of Agriculture _ (Mr. Gardiner). I never see any violent criticism of these hon. gentlemen. If a union or national government were formed, whom would my hon. friends put in their places? Would they take these hon. members out?
I am a labour man, Mr. Speaker, and I confess quite frankly that I have always been opposed to compulsion. I am still opposed to it, but there comes a time when one must bury some of the things he has always cherished, and I believe this is that time. It is my intention to vote for this bill; and if tomorrow I am advised by the ministers who are charged with responsibility and who are in possession of all the information, that conscription is necessary, then I am prepared to vote for that also.
I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the Japanese situation in British Columbia, but I shall not detain the house long. When the regulations were set up in British Columbia every person of the Japanese race within the protected area was supposed to be in his place of residence between sun-down and sun-up. That, of course, applied to the protected area. Then there were regulations with respect to arms, ammunition, motor vehicles, radios, cameras and the like. I understand that those regulations are not being carried out in British Columbia.
I am not blaming the government for that;
I believe that is the fault of the commission, and I shall not say much more on that subject.
However, I hold in my hand a copy of a train order issued to the engineers and conductors on the Canadian National railway running north from Kamloops, through the Blue river district, where the Japanese camps are situated. This order states:
Account Japanese out of hand and liable to do damage to railway; run carefully and keep sharp lookout in vicinity of Gosnell.
I also have a letter from a man who says that when the Japs were out of hand they went toward a house in that neighbourhood. There was only one woman in the house, and she promptly unlimbered a 30.30 and said that if they came another step farther there *would be some dead Japanese. This man makes a comment, "That is the first Jap retreat recorded in British Columbia". I have other letters of a similar nature, but since my time is short, I shall not refer to them in detail. In conclusion, I appeal to members of the house for unity. If there ever was a time in the history of Canada when unity was required, that time is now. To my English-speaking friends I would say this: I would urge that you have more tolerance, and that you consider the conditions existing in Switzerland, a nation of four million people and four recognized languages. In that country one hears German, French, Italian and other Romance languages. Yet, despite the difference in language there is a wonderful spirit of unity in that country. I can see no reason why we in Canada cannot have the same spirit.
To my French-speaking friends, in the most kindly spirit I would advocate the teaching of English in their schools. At the same time I would advocate the teaching of French in English schools, in order that we may get to know each other better. In my opinion, the maintenance of unity will be one of the greatest contributing factors to our share of winning the war and establishing an enduring peace.
I am sorry I have taken up so much of the time of the house. Like the speaker who preceded me, I have not in any way attempted to offend anyone. If inadvertently I have

Mobilization Act-Mr. Gauthier
done so, I hope hon. members will bear in mind that I have sat here for five months listening to speeches, and there have been occasions when I thought some of the observations were directed against me. Possibly some hon. members may think my words have been directed against them; I can assure them that is not so.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so many things have been said during the course of this debate, the most unusual I have witnessed in the sixteen consecutive sessions in which I have taken part since 1927, that one cannot speak without repeating what [DOT]has been said before by the goodly number of orators who have taken part in the discussion.
The debate on Bill No. 80 has drawn attention to the house, and seems to have caused the formation of so many groups and the expression of so many points of view that one would think we were in the Palais Bourbon when there existed from ten to fifteen different groups or parties. I doubt that this house is as noisy as the Palais Bourbon was in those days, but when one sees such a mixture of opinion, and notes the different shades of expression of those opinions on one subject he realizes it would have been very difficult at the beginning to pick a winner.
Now that we have heard from the three defence ministers, one can say with confidence that Bill No. 80, when adopted, means conscription in the near future. After three years of controversy on that question, one is now permitted to say that those who from the beginning feared that parliament was heading toward conscription for overseas service were quite right in their deduction. Conscription has long been looked upon by a minority in the house and contrary as the quintessence of total war. The fact that Australia has not adopted a measure of compulsory service for overseas service and that Northern Ireland is on the same footing does not mean anything to that minority. However, who will say that Australia is dragging behind the others? Someone has said that our allies have conscription. True-China, to defend her territory; Russia to repel the Hun; the United States to defend its colonies and its own territory. We have conscription to defend our own territory; why must we have conscription for overseas service? Hundreds of thousands of soldiers are overseas following voluntary enlistment. More are training to prepare themselves. If there had not been so much talk on the part of that troublesome minority which, with a strong press campaign and the help of its two hundred gilded friends 
in Toronto, has put the heat on the government, there would be more volunteers training for overseas. All this proves that my hon. friends have made an enormous mistake, and that their blindness when considering the subject of total war has led them to miscalculate the results they were so keen to obtain. I will not go as far as to say that this was done purposely to stop voluntary enlistments. When I speak of minorities, I do so intentionally because I am positive that the majority of our population of any descent is against conscription. They have demonstrated clearly their intention of giving a total effort on a voluntary basis, and they have demonstrated that they understand the situation in which the nations of the world are at present.
I am one of the eleven Liberal members who went to their electors in Quebec during the plebiscite campaign and urged a negative answer to the question placed before them for their consideration. We said that an affirmative vote would open the door widely to compulsion for overseas service, and I believe that we were right. The people of Quebec cast their vote against conscription; my constituency voted against it by an overwhelming majority. I do not need any further expression of their opinion in order to vote against this bill.
We have been called extremists, fifth columnists, quislings, and many other names, all of which we do not mind. The result in Quebec was conclusive. Quebec did not want to relieve the government from its commitments. While the majority of Canada answered "yes," only those to whom the commitments were made could release the government. That was our stand on the plebiscite, and it still is. That is also the stand of the province of Quebec. If we were isolationists before, we were forced to abandon that. If we were opposed to participation in any external war, we had to concede, and that is not the first time we have made concessions. But on this occasion we had the solemn promise of our leaders, and of the Conservative candidates as well, that conscription would never be imposed. We kept our promise, and we accepted the adoption of conscription after participation had been decided upon, but we are now asked to go further and accept compulsory conscription for overseas service. I do not think that is fair.
The deletion of section 3 of this aot will constitute an acceptance of the principle, and then the democratic procedure of an order in council can consummate the tragedy. I think I am right in saying thait two-thirds of the

Mobilization Act-Mr. Gauthier
members admit that conscription is not necessary, that the volunteer makes a better soldier. Nevertheless day by day we come closer to the adoption of that measure. It is no good; but the government, yielding to the pressure of the conscriptionist minority at any cost, has brought forward this bill for the deletion of section 3. I think we must admit that this is dangerous politico-mental gymnastics.
It has been said that the people of Quebec oppose conscription because they have not been properly educated on the question of war; that they do not realize that the situation is so serious; that they have not been spoken to boldly enough and so forth. Prior to 1917 we had not been told for the past twenty-five years that we would have conscription. I am not overlooking the campaign of the Nationalists. It is a positive fact that that campaign was subsidized by Tory money. But even though we had not been told for twenty-five years that we would have conscription, Quebec was still strongly opposed to conscription for overseas service, and the fact that France was then our ally did not lessen our opposition to conscription.
We have always been ready to help, to fight voluntarily. I do not need to recall the various occasions when French Canadians have fought to keep this country for England. They did it voluntarily and with enthusiasm, but they do not like broken promises. That is one good feature of their education.
One sad aspect of this change of policy is the fact that recruits have been called up and are now training for Canada's defence. From the beginning they have been under the impression that there would be no conscription for overseas service, but they are now facing the fact that with the passing of just one order in council they will be liable to be sent anywhere in the world. What will they think then of the word of honour of their representatives? What will they think then of their democratic parliament? Will there be left in them any confidence in this parliament?
The Conservative party is stamped with conscription, and this country is soon to enjoy the sight of a Liberal party with the same black spot upon its soul. Then the Tories will have the Liberal party where they have always wanted it. As their leader said before the plebiscite, they put on the heat. I understand that this go-between measure was to appease the ire of the imperialists, those within the Liberal party as well as those without. To those who believe that imperialism is dead, I ask, "Why are we denied a national flag and a national anthem?" Just because imperialists are afraid that the Canadian people will take
too much interest in the flag, a flag which would mean our whole history, a flag which would speak to the soul of our people and make them feel proud of their land. They would believe that at last they are heading toward a real national status.
Someone might answer that it would not mean much. I think that shows a lack of psychology, a lack of national pride. What is behind all this is imperialism which stands aloof behind words such as these: "Canada a nation," "autonomy," "free association of countries in the commonwealth," "freedom to declare war on anyone," "the Westminster statute," and so forth. But when it comes to the consecration of all these statutes, the red light is on and we remain a colony; a country within another country, separated by a few thousand miles of water, from which mainland we have to borrow a flag and a national anthem. They say imperialism is dead. Imperialism will never die as long as trade and commerce interests exist in the world. It will never die because England must have an empire in order to live. I know that those who stress the adoption of a national flag and a national anthem, those who do not look upon the union jack as their national flag or who do not consider "God Save the King" as their national anthem will be considered as being anti-British or even traitors. These are labelled arguments, always in stock.
The development of patriotism does not go with coercion or the denial of autonomous moves and privileges. Minorities in the world, even majorities with a mental inferiority complex, have been kept under the ferrule; and the results attained were often opposite. Sooner or later they woke up to reality. Sooner or later they realized that they were grown-up nations and were entitled to the stature of a nation. Nobody can overlook that law of centuries. Canada has over three centuries of existence. A country like ours, with unlimited wealth, has the right to its own economic and political life, and to make its own decisions. It has a right to salute its own flag and sing its national anthem, and those who would deny these priviliges have a great deal to add to their Canadianism.
I have said before in this house that the lords of the British Admiralty have never favoured a local defence progamme. At the very beginning of this war Hore-Belisha clearly expressed the same policy. If we had not been a part of the British empire, would we have declared war on European nations at the very beginning, when we were not attacked, and when nobody could foresee that this war would develop into a world war? If we had

Mobilization Act-Mr. Gauthier
just been a nation of America without any imperial bonds, we would not have acted so quickly. But when England declares war, all the free nations of the commonwealth declare war, because of their empire bonds. This fact was clearly demonstrated when Canada sent a contingent to south Africa to fight the Boers.
Since the outbreak of this war we have witnessed empires against empires. On one side, Germany, Italy and Japan wish to build up their empire at the expense of Russia, whose dream of ruling the world through communist theories is a kind of imperialism; on the other, the United States and England wish to save their empires. Everyone will admit that the united nations had to put into effect methods that were already in favour amongst totalitarian states, such as defence regulations, press censorship, compulsory loans and so forth, but with a difference in their philosophy.
I do not believe it would be a criticism of the Canadian defence regulations to say that the newspapers and people of England enjoy a larger freedom to djscuss the events of the war than we do in Canada. The defence of democracy and of Christian civilization was later on engrafted, however queer may be the fact that the seat of Catholicism is in Italy and that the armies of an atheist state are fighting on our side.
In the democratic states the parliament is elected and empowered by the people and should, normally speaking, bear the responsibilities attached to their mandate. I admit that a plebiscite is a very handy way of lessening to a certain extent responsibility toward the people. "Yes" or "no" would have been more explicit.
There wras no plebiscite when through its delegate this country signed a pact giving its word of honour that every economic and military resource would be put at the disposal of every one of the united nations whose signature appeared on that very important document called the Atlantic charter. Every economic and military resource meant all the money, munitions, foodstuffs and soldiers that Canada could provide. This parliament was not consulted on that question; nor were the Canadian people consulted, yet Canada was bound even to conscription if such a measure should be considered absolutely necessary. Even if conscription would provide but a few thousand men, we were bound by our signature to impose the conscription of men as well as the conscription of wealth. That agreement was siped on January 1, 1942, before the plebiscite. If the plebiscite was held to rectify
TMr. Gauthier.)
this act of our government, everyone will admit that, even if it was a handy way, it was not the gesture of what we would call responsible government to ask for ratification after the country had pledged itself.
Have we ever heard a member of this house urging upon this government the imposition of conscription for overseas service because we had been bound by our signature to the Atlantic charter? No. Then I am right in saying that conscription is looked upon by some, not to honour a pledge to the united nations, not as an inevitable step in providing the united nations with all the men we could get through conscription, but as part of a policy which has been strongly put forward since right after the election of 1940 by a group of men whose imperialism is as vivid as ever and for whom no conscription in Canada for overseas service would bring dishonour to this country. Canada for them is one with the empire. The boundaries of our country are the boundaries of the empire. In a word, it is the same country. Yet some will say that imperialism is dead!
With some people talk of the war effort and of conscription develops into what medical men call a neurosis, and when controversy awakens they are scandalized to hear someone advocating the defence of Canada as our primary goal. If Canada is attacked directly on its own territory it is because, in their view, we have not conscription for overseas service. The sight of Australia bringing back her soldiers to defend Australian soil does not lessen _ their "mother knows all" attitude. Conscription for overseas service has become a fixed idea with them, and since French Canadians are strongly opposed to it, queer words are uttered. But we let them go by, ready to forgive, but never ready to surrender.
Our patience has surmounted many obstacles. Our faith in our country has long made us believe that some day the minorities will see their privileges equitably considered. In war time the French Canadians are urged to contribute their share in the conscription of blood. But do you not think, sir, that their good-will would be more apparent if in peace time they were not so often deprived of their share of the advantages to which they are entitled? And this is the real situation in peace time.
"Why don't you speak English in Quebec?" someone said in this house last week. In Quebec we learn and speak both languages because both are official. We would not learn or speak English if we wanted to dominate other parts of the country. A wonderful example of tolerance is given to the "one language, one school" apostle by Switzerland.

Mobilization Act

Mr. Macmillan
They have three official languages in that country, and since none of the three try to absorb the others they are enjoying perfect unity. Why not follow the example of Quebec where the two languages are spoken freely, where religions are taught to children, and school commissions are equally subsidized by the government. That French Catholic legislature of Quebec! The example is on the threshold of the door: "open it wide and broad-mindedness will come in". That is what we find in that "depressed minority of Quebec". If our social laws are not adequate to the needs of our people, which is far from being the truth, Christian charity comes to the rescue.
We have the best laws of hygiene that one can wish. I admit that our farming has not developed into an industry and that we do not receive the millions inherent to the wheat policy. But the permanency of our farm owners is certainly better established. We do not mind buying for millions of dollars even from Toronto firms. One of them, whose president was among the two hundred, showers the province with its catalogues every year. We are patient. Our past illustrates the degree it can attain. It kept us fighting for our share in this Canada of ours. We received it from our mothers, the symbol of patience and selfsacrifice. From them we have inherited the belief in the sanctity of pledges.
We are not opposing conscription because our men are afraid to fight. It is because there is a principle at stake. For this principle we will go on and fight. But there is a limit to everything.
To those who are afraid that French Canada wants to dominate, to rule, to dictate to other parts of the country, I will read these few lines from an article in the publication "Food for Thought". It is entitled, "What French Canadians Want-Survival, not Domination", and is written by the Abbe Arthur Maheux! He says:
How English-speaking Canadians could feai domination by French Canadians has often beer a source of wonder to me. Such people shoulc read French-Canadian writers, poets, journalists and scholars. They should listen to French Canadian speeches, sermons and radio talks. ] would dare say that not a single French Cana dian has ever expressed the aim or desire oi domination in Canada or North America. St far as I know from conversations with peoph from all social groups in French Canada, tht idea of domination is quite absent from tht mind of the French Canadian. His ambition it not to dominate Canada. Even if he shoulc outnumber the other racial groups put togetkei he would not use his numerical strength tc dominate.
Those who are afraid of us should meet us more frequently and know us.
I must repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I shall vote against this bill, and do so with pleasure, because I know now that I was not mistaken about the plebiscite campaign. I know that I was right when I urged my people to vote "no", that this plebiscite meant conscription, and that the deletion of section 3, as has been said in this house, is the logical consequence of the vote. We were right when we said that. We were called Quislings and other nice names. We do not mind. AVe knew it was conscription coming, conscription in the making, and I was pleased to see that my people voted 95 per cent "no". I shall vote against the measure, and nothing will make me vote in favour of anything heading toward conscription.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to prolong this debate, which has already, perhaps, proceeded too long. I do not wish to delay the passing of this bill, but on some of the issues involved I want to make a few comments, which will be very brief.
During the course of this discussion many extraneous topics have been introduced. I am not going to pose to-night as an evangelist of harmony, because I do not believe disharmony exists to a great extent in this country. I am not going to hold an inquest on unity, because I do not believe that unity is dead or is in danger of death. I am not going to turn back very far in the pages of history. I believe that in this debate far too much emphasis has been placed on alleged disunity, and strange pictures have been painted. With all respect, may I say I think there has been far too much beating of dead political horses.
I am going to vote for this legislation. The bill before us is the result of a people's decision, a popular vote, a popular voice. That decision was made on April 27 last. While overwhelmingly in the affirmative, it was not unanimous. There was difference of opinion in every city, in every town, in every district. That difference does not mean revolt or disunity, it does not mean hatred. In these troubled days that are upon us, when half the world has been forced into silence, when an effort is being made to make us all think in terms of nazism or not to think at all, surely it is a privilege-or perhaps I should say it is a luxury-to differ with those for whom I have a deep affection, and a high regard, like those who sit around me. One of the things we are fighting for to-day is the

Mobilization Act-Mr. Macmillan
liberty of difference, and that liberty of difference does not mean the severance of friendship.
There are certain sections of the press that, with a peculiar presumption, arrogate to themselves the sole anxiety for an all-out war effort. They even become armchair strategists and field marshals. I have no objection to their assuming that role if, in doing so, they do not paint an inaccurate picture of my country. We are all, inside this house and outside this house in Canada, whatever our differences may be, one in hope and in heart, and that hope is for the speedy winning of this war. The young men, young women and children with whom I come in contact in this country are each and all sentinels on duty willing to do their best for the safety and the defence of this country. Therefore let us be done with this cry of disunity and these recriminations; let us guard our tongues and our pens when we speak or write about this bill.
In my province of Prince Edward Island the plebiscite was interpreted, as I think its language intended it to be, as a request for release from a pledge which, rightly or wrongly, was given two years ago with regard to the method of raising men for overseas service. The answer to that in my province, as it was throughout Canada on the whole, was an overwhelming "yes." That did not mean necessarily, in my judgment or in the judgment of my constituents, immediate conscription. It meant this, that when the time comes that the system now in vogue fails to be an adequate defence of this dominion, then the government is given freedom and power to act in any way necessary to save this country. When that crisis comes and those obligations arise I, as a former soldier, believe that the decision will depend on the experienced advice, the expert knowledge and the considered judgment of military leaders and of the allied command. When that time comes this government must be free to act in any way necessary, and in accordance with their action or their failure to act the people will hold them responsible.
With many of my hon. friends in this house who served in the last war I believe in the voluntary system as long as it works. I believed in it in the last war. But there may come a time when the stream of men under the voluntary system will dry up. We cannot win this war without aggressiveness; aggressiveness means, casualties; casualties mean reinforcements, and reinforcements mean that troops have to be raised and sent in one way or another. I think one of the proudest things to any Canadian is the success of our

voluntary system. In my little province, small in size but great in heart, nearly 9 per cent of the entire population have enlisted for active service. If that proportion were extended throughout all Canada, we would have over a million men in the field to-day. That is true also of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. A great percentage of those men have gone into the navy. That is natural, because those boys are born and bred to the sea; each boy is drawn to the docks as boys in other provinces are drawn to the baseball parks or the movies. The young men of the martime provinces see themselves in imagination holding a flapping top-sail in the breeze or standing by a kicking wheel on some far distant ocean. So we find them going into the merchant marine or the navy. Conscription would not mean anything in my province, because there is no one left to conscript. That, I think, should be the situation throughout Canada.
I wonder if we have considered the difficulties and obstacles with which the voluntary system was faced. There must be the will for enlistment. Let me go back, from ten years before the war to the very eve of the war, to recall those days right up to 1939 when we were living in a sleep-walker's world. In that world, into the schools and colleges and universities and on the platform and, indeed, into some of our pulpits, went hawkers of utopian propaganda. These so-called leaders exploited our youth, told them to love other countries better than their own, taught them that every war was inglorious, that every hero was a fraud; they had them sign declarations that they would fight on their own terms; even the students of Oxford signed a declaration that they would not fight for king or country. We who came back from the last war tolerated that paradise of dreams; we sat silent while they sang utopian lullabies to youth. When we consider that the boys of that time, from fifteen to twenty years of age even five years ago, now from twenty to twenty-five, have-notwithstanding that attempt at innoculation given to them by so-called leaders-gone from the schools and colleges and universities in a steady stream and enlisted, with that background I sometimes wonder that they enlisted at all without compulsion. It gives me renewed faith in youth when I regard them and their sterling character. The youth of this country have been weighed in the balance many a time and have never been found wanting.
A second thing that has interfered with the will to enlist is the stream of criticism that has flowed out. I have no objection to criticism if it is fair. But ever since this war

Mobilization Act-Mr. Macmillan
broke out, a certain section of the press in this country has spread misinterpretation to deceive the Canadian people, with greater energy than any dictatorship. One man has been pursued relentlessly and maliciously in a manner before which I think future historians of Canada will stand appalled. That man is the Prime Minister of this dominion. I am not going to indulge in excessive compliment, because it always breeds suspicion, but I will say it is not for his contemporaries to judge him, and I believe that as long as this nation survives he will be remembered in the hearts of the Canadian people because of his conduct of affairs during these last few years.
One other thing I would mention is the lack of news. I do not know who is responsible for that. We hear a great deal about the desirability of more news being spread in the United States, but where we want the news is right here; the news of how the war is going, the news that a squadron of Canadian fighters was over Cologne, that a Canadian corvette limped back to port after ramming a submarine. That is of more value than all the good-will lectures and tours and visits of all the actresses in Hollywood. We are not getting that news. Our young people are asking for it. I just give that as a hint to whoever may be responsible.
Let us make no mistake about it; the crisis is coming. It may come more quickly than we think. When it does come and it may be necessary to send men overseas, let no man think we are fighting for Britain. Does anyone suggest that the Canadian boys who may be dying to-night in Alaska or the Aleutian islands are fighting for the United States? Does anyone suggest that General MacArthur's men in Australia are fighting for Britain, or that the United States troops who were reviewed by their majesties the other day are fighting for Britain? This is what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, in France, during this June month in 1897:
I am told that here in France there are people surprised at the attachment which I feel for the crown of England, and which I do not conceal. ... That double fidelity to ideas and aspirations, quite distinct, is our glory in Canada. \ve (French Canadians) are faithful to the great nation that gave us life; we are faithful to the great nation that gave us liberty.
_ That liberty is in jeopardy to-night. It is in greater danger than ever before in the history of our world. Are we going to let it die? Do we want a repetition of Lidice in Canada, where every man was shot to death, every woman raped and sent to a concentration camp, and every child sent to a propaganda school to learn how to murder his neighbours and his kinsmen? Do we want in this country a repetition of the atrocities of Hong Kong? In my part of the country when there is a forest fire we do not wait until it comes round our homestead. We go out to meet it and keep it from our precious possessions, and I believe that is true also on the prairies. There is a line in the United States national anthem which I think fits this case:
0! thus be it ever, when freemen shall stand
Between their loved homes and wild war's desolation!
Our men are out fighting to defend their homes from "war's desolation."
When this crisis comes and it is necessary to act, I hope that action will not be the calling of parliament to debate this question again. Democracy is always at a disadvantage in war time. The dictator and the tyrant act on the instant. Democracy acts by consultation, debate and discussion. Dictatorial powers in war time are necessary, if they are not usurped and if they are given to leaders by the people. That is what we have done. The people have given the government power. Why should the government call us back here to discuss this matter at great length again? Hitler will not wait. Do not blame the method; blame Hitler, because he is responsible. The other day I read an address delivered by Admiral King, commander of the United States fleet, to the cadets at Annapolis who were just leaving to go into service. That great leader told those boys three things which I wish I could spread all over Canada: "First, do your best with what you have, and remember that there is no perfection in war either in men or in equipment. Second, do not mourn or weep over the water that has gone over the dam in the past, but let your cry be, 'Where do we go from here?' Third, there are difficulties, but 'difficulties' is the name given to things we have to overcome."
One other thought. As a Canadian I deplore the aspersions cast on Quebec. I know Quebec; it has been kind to me. I know its people. Like many others in this house, my ancestors came to this country nearly 150 years ago from the highlands of Scotland. They did useful work in this country; probably the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) will say they did the most useful work of any race, and I might agree with him. They came here in search of liberty, looking for freedom to worship God, but they did not forget that the country to which they came was born of French vision, pioneered by French enterprise, colonized by French courage and blessed by French religion. We have lived in peace. The rocks from which
3780	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Macmillan
we Canadians have been hewn were of divers countries and divers races. We are not bound together, as someone has said, by reverence for a common past or a common ancestry. We are bound together by a common hope, a hope for a peaceful world, where each man will eat in safety under his own vine what he has planted, and sing the merry song of peace to all his neighbours. We in this country are not enemies; we are friends. We must not be permitted to become enemies. We must not let anything drive us apart, not even this bill, because, as I said before, I believe we are one in hope and in heart.
We are passing through dark days. They will be darker. We shall have to give up many things. We shall have to give up our leisure and devote it to the service of our country in some capacity. There will be less gasoline, less sugar, fewer tires, fewer silk stockings, and other things, but I believe we can take it as a nation. One night, 170 years ago, by a flickering camp fire, a great soldier and writer wrote these lines on a drum head, and I think they might be our lines to-day:
These are the times that try men's souls. The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.
We have this for our consolation: the more difficult the conflict, the greater will be the triumph. We are not pessimistic. I close with one further memory, which is somewhat sacred to many people in this house. It was a spring day in France in 1918; a day of yellow' sunshine, with birds singing above the mutter of the guns, with flowers creeping out among the broken walls. The road hog of Europe was on the move; his grey troops were trying to crush the British and French armies, and there came to every commander of a Canadian unit this message. Does it not sound as though it were written yesterday?
In an endeavour to reach an immediate decision the enemy has gathered all his forces and struck a mighty blow at the British army. . . .
Measures have been taken successfully to meet this German onslaught. The French have gathered a powerful army, commanded by a most able and trusted leader and this army is now moving sw'iftly to our help. Fresh British divisions are being thrown in. The Canadians are soon to be engaged. Our motor machine gun brigade has already played a most gallant part and once again covered itself with glory.
' Looking back with pride on the unbroken record of your glorious achievements, asking you to realize that today the fate of the British empire hangs in the balance, I place my trust in the Canadian corps, knowing that where Canadians are engaged there can be no giving way.

Under the orders of your devoted officers in the coming battle you will advance or fall where you stand facing the enemy. . . .
Canadians, in this fateful hour, I command you and I trust you to fight as you have ever fought w'ith all your strength, with all your determination, with all your tranquil courage. On many a hard fought field of battle you have overcome this enemy. With God's help you shall achieve victory once more.
That was a message from Sir Arthur Currie, commander of the Canadian corps. My point is this: That message was sent to us a little more than three months after the conscription election, with all its turbulent activities. Do you suppose, Mr. Speaker, that the men who listened to that and went over the top to crack the Hindenburg line were worried about conscription? The Frenchman from Three Rivers was in the centre of his platoon; on his right was a Scotsman from Cape Breton; on his left an Irishman from the Fraser Valley or Toronto, an Englishman from Victoria. One word only described them; it was the word "Canada" on their shoulders.
I believe the spirit with which those men obeyed that order is still ours in Canada. And I believe this, that if we will only banish intolerance from our minds and prejudice from our hearts, and go forward together, with God's help we, too, will achieve victory.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in this debate. First I would congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon the well-prepared, ably delivered and explicit statement he made to the house at the opening of the debate. I would congratulate, .too, the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) upon the courageous and vigorous statement he made, and the clear manner in which he placed his position, and that of Quebec, before the house. I would congratulate, too, the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) upon his clear exposition of the position of Quebec.
I congratulate the government upon the nomination of the Minister of Justice to his portfolio, because I believe the Prime Minister selected for that post one of the most capable men in Canada. May I congratulate, too, all other ministers and hon. members who have taken part in the debate. Each has expressed his views. One cannot be in favour of all he hears from the orators, but we can believe at least that these men have spoken in good faith.
I have believed since the first session of this parliament that the Conservative party, those who have supported that party and certain organizations throughout Canada, have waged an organized campaign to create preju-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Ryan
dice in the public mind against the Prime Minister. There is no doubt whatsoever as to the truth of that suggestion, and I could prove it from clippings I have taken from editorials in newspapers.
Six months after the beginning of the war there was a general election, and the leaders of both the major parties stated there was to be no conscription for overseas service. I understand some hon. members opposite did not accept the statement of their leader. That does not matter, however, because the statement was made by both leaders. At the first session of parliament the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) stated in the house that he had been chosen temporary leader, and that when he was chosen it was understood he would oppose the government. He also stated, "As long as I remain in the house I intend to oppose the government." I give him credit that that is what he has done since the first session.
There has been an organized campaign to create prejudice against the Prime Minister- not so much against the government, because it has been suggested at certain times, particularly during the first and second sessions of this parliament, that certain ministers might replace the Prime Minister, if he would kindly get out. 1 believe it was the Montreal Gazette which stated, "Now is the time for the Prime Minister to resign. He could resign in all his glory. He could be one of the best Prime Ministers Canada ever had, if he would get out now." They are of the same opinion to-day.
I recall that on January 26 one of the Ottawa daily papers published a special number in three sections. There was the regular news section, and two others in addition. One of those sections was headed "Canada's War Effort for Victory", and pointed out that the war effort of the dominion was rapidly expanding to a peak. In those special sections I found photographs of nine ministers, and five other gentlemen connected with war departments. The texts under these pictures were most appropriate, giving due credit for the urork done by each. So far as it went this was all right. But something was missing, in none of the sections was there a photograph of the Prime Minister of Canada. Why was it missing? It was missing for the reason I mentioned earlier, namely, prejudice against the Prime Minister.
If ministers of the crown have done their duty, they should receive credit. But if, for instance, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) have done their duty, then surely some of the credit must go
to the Prime Minister who had the good judgment to select those men-because we know it is the Prime Minister who made the selection. Let us give him credit. .
During the last session I said this, "We may not agree with everything that is being done by the government; but we should agree that on the whole the Prime Minister and the government are carrying on a gigantic undertaking very satisfactorily and under strict control." I repeat that to-night, because it is just as true now as it was then.
In that connection may I read an extract from Liberty of June 20, appearing under the hand of the publisher:
An executive of one of Canada's greatest industrial concerns has stated, "I wonder if people realize that they have seen a miracle. They possibly do not know it, but they have seen in Canada in the last two years the greatest per capita industrial expansion that has ever occurred to any people anywhere."
Following that statement, I should like at this time to congratulate the Minister of Munitions and Supply upon the clear statement of facts which he gave us the other day. I think he has always been held in high esteem, but he will be held in still higher esteem after making that statement. I think it was John Ruskin who wrote:
That the greatest thing a human soul ever does in this world is to see something, and tell what he saw in a plain way. Hundreds of people can talk for one who can think, but thousands can think for one who can see.
There is no argument as to where the defence line of Canada lies; the difference of opinion is in connection with the method to be used to select men to reinforce that line. In connection with conscription for overseas, I should like to read a letter which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of June 23 signed by a gentleman named Arnold Stuart. The heading on this letter, which I suppose is put there by the Gazette, is "Crerar's Convictions", and it reads:
Sir,-This morning's leading editorial asks some pertinent questions concerning Hon. T. A. Crerar, federal Minister of Mines and Resources. "Where are the convictions of 1917," you ask, "and where is his courage of that war?" (concerning conscription).
Well, I should say it is quite possible that Mr. Crerar has looked up the record. Perhaps you should do so too, Mr. Editor. It would show the following:
404.000	enrolments under the Military Service Act (conscription).
380.000	exemptions asked (118,000 in Ontario;
115.000	in Quebec, etc.).
104.000	exemption claims approved in Ontario;
108.000	in Quebec, and so on in other provinces.
31.000	ordered to report for duty. 5,000 of these defaulted, leaving 26,000 net yield out of
405.000	enrolled.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Ryan

It is quite possible, Mr. Editor, indeed highly probable, that Hon. Mr. Crerar and his leader the Prime Minister, have these figures of the results of conscription in mind. Is it any wonder that they want to defer conscription until every other expedient has failed?
The Gazette said in 1918 concerning the Union government's course in applying the Military Service Act (conscription):
The government appears to have established a system which, if it gets the men at all, will get them so slowly that whatever military advantage depends on expeditious reinforcement will be lost.
If, as is alleged, recruits are coming in satisfactorily under the voluntary system there would appear to be little reason to turn again to the sad expedient of 1917. The fact is that politicians on both sides have for decades made such a bete noir of conscription that now it rises up to bedevil the whole domain of our war psychology. But nothing is to be gained by ignoring the real situation.
The leader of the opposition made the following statement, as reported on page 2768 of Hansard:
Because this government in the first nine months of the war did absolutely nothing to meet the situation. They were going to have a moderate war. A moderate war! Ask any hon. member from the province of Quebec if they were not promised that Canada's contribution would be a moderate contribution.
As far as I am concerned I have no recollection, and I do not believe anyone else has, that Quebec was promised a moderate war. The promise was made to Quebec that men would not be conscripted for overseas service. Quebec has never objected to a total war effort; Quebec has never objected to men enrolling voluntarily to go any place in the world. Quebec has not criticized the all-out war effort, and it did not criticize the billion dollar gift to England for food, materials and so on. Quebec has not criticized the budget or anything else. There has been no criticism of the government or of any action that has been taken in furthering our total war effort. But the people of Quebec were promised, and they want the government to keep the promise that there will be no conscription for service overseas.
There is one thing I have had in mind for a long time, but hon. members who have spoken before me have brought this up. I am in favour of increased pay for the men in the armed forces. I am also in favour of widowed mothers whose only sons have enlisted being given the same allowance as that received by a wife, namely, $35 a month. To-day such a widowed mother receives only $20. The men who are fighting for our liberty must be assured that after the war there will be a better world in which to live, a world in which every man will be guaranteed work and security.

I want to congratulate the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) upon some of the public statements he has made during the last couple of years. I do not know if the government was aware of all these statements, but I am very much in favour of certain of the things which the Minister of Pensions and National Health thinks should be done after this war is over. In this connection I should like to quote from "The Road We are Travelling 1914-1942" by Stuart Chase. No doubt most hon. members know who Mr. Chase is. He is a writer on economic questions, and in this book which has just been published, he said:
I believe, moreover, that we are more likely to win the war if we have a clear idea of goals for the peace. Men fight better when they know for what they are fighting. Any peace we make must be superior to that which our enemies can offer. They make alluring promises about new orders and new spheres of prosperity. These promises are widely heard in the lands most affected, and we shall have to do more than sneer at them. We shall have to-and can-offer something better, more just and more convincing.
Defeatism about the peace is almost as dangerous as defeatism about the war. The victory need not and must not lead to economic depression and disaster at home. Actually, when peace does come, it will be an opportunity and a challenge; an opportunity to use our vastly increased plant and human resources to raise the standard of living for us all; a challenge to make a greater civilization.
If our young men were assured that there would be a new and better world after this war, they might feel like joining up.
There are a number of things I should like to say with regard to the plebiscite, and I should like to give my understanding of the plebiscite vote. First, I understand it as a vote to release the government from the promise they had given to the people of Canada that men would not be conscripted for service overseas. Second, the plebiscite was the only democratic method by which the government could secure an expression of opinion from the people in regard to their promise. Third, the "yes" vote in eight provinces did release the government from their promise. However, this vote cannot be interpreted as a definite and emphatic vote for conscription but should be interpreted as a vote for freedom of action for the government. Fourth, the "no" vote refused to release the government from their promise. This vote must be understood as a definite and emphatic vote against conscription of men for service overseas. Fifth, if Bill No. 80 is adopted by parliament, it is my opinion that should the government find it necessary to impose con-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bonnier
scription of men for overseas service, the matter should be submitted to parliament for final decision.
It has not been proven up to the present that the voluntary method of enrolling men has not been satisfactory and that, if there had been conscription of men for overseas service, a greater number of men could have been trained and equipped. I never heard that any of the three defence ministers were not satisfied with enrolments under the voluntary system. I understood that some time ago the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) stated that he believed that with the voluntary system the country could carry on until March, 1943. I think some hon. members misunderstood the three speeches made by the ministers of defence and were under the impression that they were in favour of immediate conscription. But these three ministers did not say one word against the voluntary system. They did not say that the voluntary system had failed; they did not say or suggest that conscription should be imposed at once. They did say -that they would vote for the bill. Undoubtedly the ministers of defence will vote for the bill or, like the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), they would have to resign from the government. There is no doubt in my mind that when these ministers find it necessary to impose conscription for overseas service they will be in favour of imposing it, but in their speeches they did not say anything about that. The public also are under the impression that the voluntary system has been satisfactory, and nothing has been said up to this time by the ministers of defence against that system.
The "no" vote in Quebec was not a vote intended to disrupt the bonne entente that has existed between the two races that have built up Canada. It was a vote to uphold a principle which is deeply rooted in the minds of the great majority of the electors of Quebec.
The vote on the plebiscite or on Bill No. 80 should not affect the good work that has been done up to the present to cement Canadian unity, and this good work should be continued.
Let me recall to this house the words which the Prime Minister uttered in Winnipeg on July 10, 1941. He said:
My duty as I see it is to seek above all else to preserve national unity, for on the maintenance of national unity all else depends.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say as a Quebecker to the English-speaking members of this house that I do not think we shall find men who have more consideration for the English-speaking members than the members from Quebec, and I say to all the English-speaking members of all the other 44561-239J
provinces that I do not believe the people of their constituencies have any better friends than the people of Quebec. I am persuaded that I can also say with equal assurance to the members from Quebec that they could not find any better friends than the Englishspeaking members from the other provinces, whose constituents also, I am sure, have the same friendly feeling toward the people of Quebec as the people of Quebec have towards them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT TO SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if we really need conscription in this country more than in any other British colony. Many voters have asked me this question: Why should Canada adopt a conscription measure which every other English colony has rejected? I would like to have a reply to that question which I have been asked repeatedly, in order to satisfy my electors and state the government's views to them. Australia, Northern Ireland, New Zealand and India have not introduced conscription. Neither has Egypt. Why then do Great Britain and Canada wish to force conscription upon us every time war is declared? Why is this? I would like to know once for all in order to be able to enlighten my constituents.
Mr. Speaker, Sir Wilfrid Laurier always endorsed voluntary service in this country. For my part, I have done the same thing ever since I cast my first ballot. We have been brought up with that in mind. It was in 1903, I think, that we had the Boer war. We dispatched a contingent of volunteers overseas but there was no conscription. Then in 1911 the Conservatives attained power largely through a platform which denounced Laurier's reciprocal trade agreement with the United States and naval programme to the province of Quebec. They tricked the Quebec population and the English element of Canada into defeating Laurier. When he appealed to the people, the English population claimed that Canada was being sold to the United States, that the intention was to annex our country to the United States. In Quebec, the mothers were told: Laurier wants to send your sons on foreign seas immediately. He wants to send your children to war as cannon fodder. He intends sending them to the China sea and to all European waters. Was that not the cry heard all through the campaign organized by the Tories of Quebec and those of Ontario and the other English-speaking provinces in order to defeat Laurier? He was defeated and on the very next day what steps were taken by the Borden government which

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bonnier
had just come into power? Instead of building a navy, we were asked to send 835 million to England.
In 1914, war was declared. Once more we contributed volunteers until 1917; but in 1916 a census was ordered. At first, the people of the French-Canadian province refused to
register. In this difficulty, the clergy were asked to undertake a campaign in the various parishes to urge the people to register, stating that it was not a matter of conscription but simply a means of ascertaining the exact population of the country. In 1917, after the census, a conscription bill was introduced. It was opposed by all French Canadians and many Britishers. Our efforts failed to convince the people of Canada that the voluntary system of enlistment was adequate. At that time, many supporters of Laurier, even many of his former ministers, forsook him. But he remained in the struggle. Ever since his attaining the office of Prime Minister, he had held to the principle of avoiding conscription and maintaining the voluntary system. To-day, after so many years during which we have been taught that the voluntary system is the better method, how can we change our views on this subject and support conscription? Our minds have been steeped in the doctrine of voluntary enlistment. In 1938, during the partial election which brought me to this house, conscription was mentioned. I carried the vote of the Liberal convention against seven candidates. Then came the election. You all know my opponent, the former mayor of Montreal, who had been elected to his post by a majority of more than 50,000 and who has always been a dangerous opponent. My election was due to the former minister of public works (Mr. Cardin) and the late Hon. Mr. Rinfret. Conscription was brought up even then, with the promise that it would never be introduced. Again in 1940, it was generally opposed. Moreover, even the English-speaking members of the other provinces were elected on the strength of anti-conscription pledges. Why have they altered their views? Their election campaign, as that of all the others, was waged on the conscription issue. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) did not come to the province of Quebec only; he visited all provinces, and so did the other ministers. Was there a speech specially prepared for the province of Quebec and another for Ontario and the maritime provinces? No; he gave everywhere the same pledge, to wit, there would be no conscription.
If I remember well, one of the previous speakers who is from Prince Edward Island and represents, I think, the constituency of Queens, (Mr. Macmillan), quoted what
{Mr. Bonnier.]
Laurier said in France when he thanked that country for having given us birth and England for having given us freedom. Supposing France were one day to be at war not with England but with any other country. Could we then advocate conscription in order to assist our former mother country? Would such a course be accepted? Yet that is a perfectly legitimate stand: one country gave us birth and the other gave us freedom. We would certainly be willing to help our former mother country on a voluntary basis, but we would never advocate compulsory military service for that purpose.
It is said that we are cowardly and that we are afraid to participate in the war. Mr. Speaker, those who say that do not remember that in 1812 our neighbours, who are now on friendly terms with us, invaded Canada. What did the French Canadians do at that time? Did they look around in order to see if the British were there? Did they wait for conscription before rising and saying: We are going to defend our country? They did not. General de Salaberry and his army set out to meet the enemy. The battle was won near Chateauguay at the spot now called Bryson, on the Chateauguay river, in my native county. A monument erected there bears the names of French Canadians who did not wait for the English to defend Canada. They took up her defence themselves. They held their ground right up to the present border on the 45th degree of latitude.
The answer to the plebiscite in the province of Quebec and the intelligent and clear sighted vote cast by her people should have been enough to open the eyes of the Prime Minister and even of the most obtuse among his colleagues. Such also should have been the effect of the resignation of the Prime Minister's faithful colleague, who has been the senior member of this house since the death of the late Mr. Lapointe and whose tact and eloquence held the Montreal district under the Prime Minister's banner as Mr. Lapointe had done in the Quebec district. The resignation of the former Minister of Public Works has therefore come as a most conclusive confirmation of our stand.
We have always believed in Mr. Cardin's sincerity and we now have more reason than ever to do so. Just as Mr. Lapointe, our lamented leader, and we ourselves did, Mr. Cardin hoped that a government led by one whose very faithfulness to Laurier in his struggle against conscription had led to his being chosen as leader of the Liberal party, would never enforce such a measure. It seems that he was in such earnest about it

Privilege-Mr. O'Neill
